MURPHY.clue: Inspiratory arrest during right-upper-quadrant palpation suggests cholecystitis
MURPHY.rationale: This sign supports acute cholecystitis. Keep the patient fasting and get imaging.

MCMURRAY.clue: A click with joint-line pain during knee rotation suggests a meniscus tear
MCMURRAY.rationale: Rotation tests load the meniscus. A negative test does not fully clear it.

LACHMAN.clue: A soft end point when the tibia is drawn forward suggests an ACL tear
LACHMAN.rationale: The This finding test is preferred acutely because hamstrings guard the drawer test.

PHALEN.clue: Wrist flexion that numbs the radial fingers suggests carpal tunnel
PHALEN.rationale: This finding and Tinel support median compression. Thenar weakness is a later finding.

TINEL.clue: Tapping a nerve that tingles distally suggests irritation at that site
TINEL.rationale: This finding is used at the carpal tunnel, cubital tunnel, and tarsal tunnel.

BABINSKI.clue: An upgoing toe in an adult is an upper motor neuron sign
BABINSKI.rationale: This finding is normal in infants and abnormal in adults.

ROMBERG.clue: Falling only after the eyes close points to proprioceptive loss
ROMBERG.rationale: This finding is positive when balance fails only with the eyes closed.

ASTERIXIS.clue: A flapping tremor of the extended wrists suggests metabolic encephalopathy
ASTERIXIS.rationale: This finding is classic in hepatic encephalopathy.

KUSSMAUL.clue: Deep rapid breathing compensates for a metabolic acidosis such as DKA
KUSSMAUL.rationale: This finding respirations are a respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis.

STRIDOR.clue: A high-pitched inspiratory sound means the upper airway is in danger
STRIDOR.rationale: This finding is upper-airway obstruction. Do not leave the patient.

WHEEZING.clue: A musical expiratory sound means narrowed lower airways
WHEEZING.rationale: A silent chest after wheeze can mean almost no air is moving.

CRACKLES.clue: Inspiratory sounds from fluid or opening of collapsed alveoli
CRACKLES.rationale: Basilar This finding in failure do not clear with a cough the way atelectasis may.

DULLNESS.clue: A flat percussion note suggests fluid or consolidation under the chest wall
DULLNESS.rationale: Percussion This finding is compared with the other side.

EGOPHONY.clue: An E-to-A change over a consolidated lobe
EGOPHONY.rationale: This finding, bronchophony, and whispered pectoriloquy cluster over consolidation.

CLUBBING.clue: Bulbous fingertips that develop with chronic lung or cyanotic heart disease
CLUBBING.rationale: This finding takes time. It is not an acute finding.

CYANOSIS.clue: Blue color from unsaturated hemoglobin, a late sign of hypoxemia
CYANOSIS.rationale: Central This finding involves the tongue and lips.

ORTHOPNEA.clue: Breathlessness when lying flat, classic in left-sided heart failure

DYSPNEA.clue: The symptom of breathlessness, which is assessed before it is called anxiety
DYSPNEA.rationale: This finding is what the patient feels. Measure it.

HEMOPTYSIS.clue: Coughing blood can mean tuberculosis, cancer, or pulmonary embolism
HEMOPTYSIS.rationale: Massive This finding threatens the airway.

ANGINA.clue: Exertional chest pressure relieved by rest suggests myocardial ischemia
ANGINA.rationale: Rest pain or prolonged pain is an acute coronary syndrome, not stable This finding.

ISCHEMIA.clue: Tissue demand for oxygen that exceeds supply
ISCHEMIA.rationale: Troponin separates injury from This finding alone.

INFARCT.clue: Tissue death from prolonged loss of blood flow
INFARCT.rationale: Time to reperfusion determines how much muscle is lost.

TROPONIN.clue: The preferred blood marker of myocardial injury
TROPONIN.rationale: This finding is more specific than older CK-MB testing.

STEMI.clue: ST-elevation infarction that needs immediate reperfusion
STEMI.rationale: Door-to-balloon time is the systems goal.

MURMUR.clue: A sound of turbulent flow graded and timed in the cardiac cycle
MURMUR.rationale: Systolic murmurs are common; diastolic murmurs are abnormal.

GALLOP.clue: An extra heart sound; S3 suggests volume overload and S4 a stiff ventricle
GALLOP.rationale: S3 can be normal in young people and pregnancy.

JVD.clue: Visible neck veins from high right-sided filling pressure
JVD.rationale: Assess jugular veins with the head of the bed raised.

EDEMA.clue: Swelling from fluid in the interstitial space
EDEMA.rationale: Daily weight tracks This finding better than a single measurement.

ASCITES.clue: Fluid in the abdomen, often from portal hypertension
ASCITES.rationale: Shifting dullness is the bedside test.

JAUNDICE.rationale: Scleral icterus is often noticed first.

MELENA.clue: Black tarry stool from digested blood, usually an upper GI bleed
MELENA.rationale: Iron also darkens stool but does not make it tarry and foul in the same way.

REBOUND.clue: Pain when abdominal pressure is released, a peritoneal sign
REBOUND.rationale: This finding is one peritoneal sign, interpreted with vitals.

GUARDING.clue: Involuntary abdominal wall tightness over inflammation
GUARDING.rationale: Voluntary This finding can be distracted; involuntary cannot.

ROVSING.clue: Right-lower-quadrant pain when the left side is pressed, suggesting appendicitis
ROVSING.rationale: This finding is supportive, not required, for the diagnosis.

PSOAS.clue: Pain with hip extension that suggests an irritated This finding, as in appendicitis
PSOAS.rationale: The This finding sign is one of the appendicitis signs.

OBTURATOR.clue: Pain with internal rotation of the flexed hip, a pelvic appendicitis sign
OBTURATOR.rationale: It is not a standalone diagnosis.

COURVOISIER.clue: A painless palpable gallbladder with jaundice suggests malignancy, not a stone
COURVOISIER.rationale: This finding law is about malignant biliary obstruction.

GREYTURNER.clue: Flank bruising that can appear in severe pancreatitis
GREYTURNER.rationale: Grey Turner and Cullen signs are late and uncommon.

CULLEN.clue: Periumbilical bruising from retroperitoneal or intraperitoneal bleeding
CULLEN.rationale: This finding sign is associated with hemorrhagic pancreatitis.

SPIDER.clue: Angiomata on the trunk that suggest chronic liver disease
SPIDER.rationale: A few spiders can be normal, especially in pregnancy.

CAPUT.clue: Dilated abdominal wall veins from portal hypertension
CAPUT.rationale: This finding medusae radiate from the umbilicus.

FETOR.clue: A sweet breath odor of hepatic encephalopathy
FETOR.rationale: This finding hepaticus is supportive, not diagnostic alone.

VARICES.clue: Dilated esophageal veins that bleed in portal hypertension
VARICES.rationale: Nonselective beta blockers and banding prevent rebleeding.

CIRRHOSIS.clue: End-stage liver fibrosis with portal hypertension and synthetic failure
CIRRHOSIS.rationale: Synthetic function is albumin and INR, not the transaminases.

HEPATITIS.clue: Liver inflammation; A is fecal-oral and B and C are blood-borne
HEPATITIS.rationale: ALT rises more than ALP in hepatocellular injury.

CHOLELITH.clue: Gallstones that cause biliary colic when they obstruct the cystic duct
CHOLELITH.rationale: Fever and a constant pain mean cholecystitis or cholangitis, not simple colic.

CHOLANGITIS.clue: Biliary infection with fever, jaundice, and right-upper-quadrant pain
CHOLANGITIS.rationale: Reynolds pentad adds hypotension and confusion.

COLITIS.clue: Colonic inflammation with diarrhea, from infection, ischemia, or inflammatory bowel disease
COLITIS.rationale: C. difficile is considered after antibiotics.

CELIAC.clue: Gluten-sensitive enteropathy with foul stools and iron deficiency
CELIAC.rationale: Diagnosis is serology and biopsy while the patient is still eating gluten.

CROHN.clue: Transmural gut inflammation that can occur anywhere and skips segments

COLITISUC.clue: Continuous mucosal inflammation starting in the rectum

IBS.clue: Pain with bowel-habit change and no alarm features or structural disease
IBS.rationale: Alarm features such as bleeding or night symptoms need investigation.

GERD.clue: Heartburn from reflux of acid, worse lying down after meals

ULCER.clue: A break in the stomach or duodenal lining, often from H. pylori or NSAIDs
ULCER.rationale: Duodenal pain may improve with food; gastric pain may worsen.

HPYLORI.clue: A bacterium that causes ulcers and raises gastric cancer risk
HPYLORI.rationale: Test of cure is used after treatment in many protocols.

GIARDIASIS.clue: Greasy foul diarrhea after contaminated water
GIARDIASIS.rationale: Treatment is an appropriate antiprotozoal, not an antibacterial by default.

WHIPPLE.clue: Malabsorption, arthritis, and neurologic disease from Tropheryma
WHIPPLE.rationale: It is treated with antibiotics that enter the CNS.

WILSON.clue: Copper accumulation causing liver disease and a movement disorder in a young person
WILSON.rationale: Kayser-Fleischer rings are copper in the cornea.

ALPHAONE.clue: Antitrypsin deficiency that causes early emphysema and liver disease

EMPHYSEMA.clue: Permanent enlargement of air spaces with destruction of their walls

ASTHMA.clue: Reversible airway obstruction with wheeze, cough, or chest tightness
ASTHMA.rationale: A controller inhaler is added when rescue use is frequent.

BRONCHIECT.clue: Permanently dilated bronchi with copious daily sputum
BRONCHIECT.rationale: Airway clearance is a core treatment.

PNEUMONIA.clue: Infection of the lung parenchyma with fever, cough, and a new infiltrate
PNEUMONIA.rationale: Severity scores decide who leaves the clinic.

PLEURISY.clue: Sharp chest pain that worsens with a deep breath
PLEURISY.rationale: A friction rub supports pleural inflammation.

TENSION.clue: Pneumothorax that shifts the mediastinum and drops the blood pressure
TENSION.rationale: Needle decompression is a bridge to a chest tube.

EFFUSION.clue: Fluid between the lung and the chest wall
EFFUSION.rationale: Lights criteria separate exudate from transudate.

SARCOIDOSIS.clue: Noncaseating granulomas, often with bilateral hilar adenopathy
SARCOIDOSIS.rationale: Hypercalcemia can occur from granuloma vitamin D activity.

FIBROSIS.clue: Scarring of the lung that causes dry crackles and a restrictive pattern
FIBROSIS.rationale: Clubbing is common in idiopathic pulmonary This finding.

SILICOSIS.clue: Fibrotic lung disease of miners and sandblasters with upper-lobe nodules

ASBESTOSIS.clue: Interstitial disease and pleural plaques after shipyard or construction exposure

HEARTFAIL.clue: Syndrome of congestion and low output from a heart that cannot meet demand
HEARTFAIL.rationale: Daily weights and sodium advice are core counseling.

FLUTTER.clue: Atrial tachycardia with a sawtooth pattern, often conducting at a fixed ratio
FLUTTER.rationale: Anticoagulation rules resemble those of fibrillation.

SVT.clue: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia from above the ventricle
SVT.rationale: Vagal maneuvers are tried when the patient is stable.

BRADYCARDIA.clue: A slow heart rate that matters when the patient is hypotensive or symptomatic
BRADYCARDIA.rationale: Atropine is the first drug for symptomatic This finding in the usual algorithm.

BLOCK.clue: Failure of conduction from sinus node to ventricle, graded as first, second, or third
BLOCK.rationale: Symptomatic high-grade This finding needs pacing.

TAMPONADE.clue: Compression of the heart by pericardial fluid, with low pressure and distended neck veins
TAMPONADE.rationale: Fluids are a bridge to drainage.

MYOCARDITIS.clue: Inflammation of heart muscle, often after a virus, mimicking infarction
MYOCARDITIS.rationale: Supportive care and avoiding exercise are typical early advice.

AORTICDISS.clue: Tearing chest pain radiating to the back, with unequal pulses

ANEURYSM.clue: A dilated artery that can rupture, classically the abdominal aorta
ANEURYSM.rationale: Smoking is the dominant modifiable risk.

DVT.clue: A clot in a deep leg vein, suspected with unilateral swelling
DVT.rationale: Do not massage a suspected clot.

EMBOLISM.clue: A clot or other material that travels and blocks a distant vessel
EMBOLISM.rationale: Prevention is mobility and prophylaxis in the hospital.

STROKE.clue: Sudden neurologic deficit from ischemia or hemorrhage
STROKE.rationale: Time windows decide thrombolysis and thrombectomy.

TIA.clue: A transient focal deficit with no infarction on imaging
TIA.rationale: It is not a small seizure by default.

HEMORRHAGE.clue: Bleeding into tissue; in the head it often presents with sudden headache and vomiting
HEMORRHAGE.rationale: Blood pressure control and reversal of anticoagulation matter.

SUBARACH.clue: Bleeding into the cerebrospinal fluid space, with a thunderclap headache
SUBARACH.rationale: A negative CT early still may need a lumbar puncture.

SUBDURAL.clue: Venous bleeding under the dura, often after a minor fall in an older adult

EPIDURAL.clue: Arterial bleeding from a skull fracture, with a lucid interval

MENINGITIS.clue: Fever, neck stiffness, and headache from inflamed meninges
MENINGITIS.rationale: Droplet precautions apply until bacterial disease is treated.

MIGRAINE.clue: A unilateral throbbing headache with nausea or light sensitivity
MIGRAINE.rationale: New worst headache is not labeled This finding first.

CLUSTER.clue: Severe orbital pain in bursts, with tearing and a runny nose
CLUSTER.rationale: Oxygen and a triptan are acute treatments.

SEIZURE.clue: A sudden abnormal electrical discharge, which may convulse or only stare
SEIZURE.rationale: Status epilepticus is continuous This finding activity and is an emergency.

SYNCOPE.clue: A brief loss of consciousness from low cerebral perfusion
SYNCOPE.rationale: A prodrome of warmth and nausea is more reflex.

VERTIGO.clue: A spinning sensation, either peripheral or central
VERTIGO.rationale: Hearing loss and tinnitus point to the ear.

PARKINSON.clue: Resting tremor, rigidity, and slow small movements
PARKINSON.rationale: Falls and autonomic features come later.

ESSENTIAL.clue: A bilateral action tremor, often of the hands and head, improved by alcohol

HUNTINGTON.clue: Chorea and behavior change in a family pattern, from a CAG repeat
HUNTINGTON.rationale: Genetic counseling is required before testing.

ALZHEIMER.clue: Progressive memory loss that interferes with daily function
ALZHEIMER.rationale: Sudden confusion is delirium, not a new dementia.

DELIRIUM.clue: Acute fluctuating confusion that is a medical symptom
DELIRIUM.rationale: It is not treated with a sedative as the first move.

DEMENTIA.rationale: Screening is followed by a reversible-cause check.

MYASTHENIA.clue: Fatigable weakness, often of the eyes, that worsens through the day

GUILLAIN.clue: Ascending paralysis after an infection, with areflexia
GUILLAIN.rationale: Reflexes are lost, unlike in a spinal cord lesion.

BOTULISM.clue: Descending paralysis with dilated pupils, from a toxin that blocks acetylcholine release

LAMBERT.clue: Proximal weakness that improves with repeated effort, associated with small-cell lung cancer
LAMBERT.rationale: It is the opposite of myasthenia, which fatigues.

CARPAL.clue: Median nerve compression causing nocturnal hand numbness
CARPAL.rationale: Splints and activity change come before surgery in mild disease.

ROTATOR.clue: Cuff pain with overhead reach and night pain
ROTATOR.rationale: Weakness out of proportion to pain suggests a tear.

IMPINGEMENT.clue: Pain as the arm passes through the middle of abduction

FROZEN.clue: Shoulder that loses external rotation and then all motion
FROZEN.rationale: It passes through freezing, This finding, and thawing stages.

TENNIS.clue: Lateral elbow pain with gripping, from extensor tendon overload
TENNIS.rationale: Counterforce bracing and load reduction help.

GOLFER.clue: Medial elbow pain from flexor-pronator overload
GOLFER.rationale: It is less common than lateral elbow pain.

DEQUERVAIN.clue: Pain at the radial wrist in a tendon sheath of the thumb

TRIGGER.clue: A finger that catches and then releases
TRIGGER.rationale: Corticosteroid injection is a common first treatment.

DUPUYTREN.clue: Thickening of the palmar fascia that pulls a finger into flexion
DUPUYTREN.rationale: It is not a tendon injury.

GANGLION.clue: A fluid-filled cyst, often on the dorsum of the wrist
GANGLION.rationale: Observation is reasonable when it does not limit function.

BUNION.clue: Lateral deviation of the great toe with a medial prominence

PLANTAR.clue: Heel pain worst with the first steps of the morning
PLANTAR.rationale: Stretching and load management are first-line.

ACHILLES.clue: Posterior heel pain or a sudden pop with inability to push off
ACHILLES.rationale: The Thompson test is positive in rupture.

ANKLESPR.clue: Inversion injury that tears the lateral ligaments in order

FRACTURE.clue: A broken bone, suspected when bearing weight is impossible or the bone is tender

SEPTIC.clue: An infected joint that is hot, swollen, and held still
SEPTIC.rationale: The knee is the most common site.

GOUT.clue: An exquisitely painful red joint, classically the great toe, from urate crystals
GOUT.rationale: Urate-lowering therapy is not the treatment of the flare alone.

PSEUDOGOUT.clue: Crystal arthritis from calcium pyrophosphate, often in the knee of an older adult
PSEUDOGOUT.rationale: The joint is still tapped to exclude infection.

RHEUMATOID.clue: Symmetric small-joint arthritis with morning stiffness lasting hours

OSTEOARTH.clue: Joint pain that is worse with use and better with rest, with bony enlargement
OSTEOARTH.rationale: Brief morning stiffness separates it from inflammatory disease.

ANKYLOSING.clue: Inflammatory back pain in a young adult that improves with activity
ANKYLOSING.rationale: Extension exercise and medical therapy limit flexion deformity.

LUPUS.clue: A multisystem autoimmune disease with rash, joints, and serositis

SCLERODERMA.clue: Thick skin and Raynaud phenomenon, with lung and kidney risk
SCLERODERMA.rationale: This finding renal crisis is a hypertensive emergency.

SJOGREN.clue: Dry eyes and dry mouth from autoimmune destruction of glands
SJOGREN.rationale: It can accompany other autoimmune disease.

POLYMYALGIA.clue: Aching shoulders and hips in an older adult, with a high sedimentation rate

GIANT.clue: Headache, jaw claudication, and vision risk in an older adult

RAYNAUD.clue: Fingers that turn white then blue then red in the cold
RAYNAUD.rationale: Ulceration or asymmetry suggests a connective-tissue disease.

DERMATITIS.clue: Inflamed skin, itchy and red, from eczema, contact, or stasis
DERMATITIS.rationale: Steroid potency is matched to the site.

PSORIASIS.clue: Well-demarcated silvery plaques on extensor surfaces

CELLULITIS.clue: A spreading warm red skin infection
CELLULITIS.rationale: Mark the border to judge spread.

SHINGLES.clue: A painful vesicular rash in one dermatome
SHINGLES.rationale: The eye branch is an ophthalmology emergency.

MELANOMA.clue: A pigmented lesion that is asymmetric, irregular, and changing

BASAL.clue: A pearly papule with telangiectasia, the common skin cancer
BASAL.rationale: It rarely metastasizes but invades locally.

SQUAMOUS.clue: A scaly or ulcerated lesion on sun-damaged skin that can metastasize

ACNE.clue: Comedones and inflammatory papules of the pilosebaceous unit

ROSACEA.clue: Central facial redness and papules without comedones

UTICARIA.clue: Transient wheals that move and itch

ANAPHYLAXIS.clue: A systemic allergic reaction with airway or shock
ANAPHYLAXIS.rationale: The thigh is the injection site.

ECZEMA.clue: Itchy flexural rash from a defective skin barrier
ECZEMA.rationale: Moisturize and use the least steroid that works.

SCABIES.clue: Intense itch, worse at night, with burrows in the finger webs
SCABIES.rationale: Treat contacts at the same time.

LICE.clue: Itching of the scalp or body with visible nits
LICE.rationale: Treat and clean combs; school policy varies.

TINIA.clue: A ring-shaped scaly patch from a dermatophyte
TINIA.rationale: Nails need longer therapy than skin.

CANDIDA.clue: A beefy red rash in moist folds, with satellite pustules
CANDIDA.rationale: Dry the area and use an antifungal.

OTITIS.clue: A bulging painful eardrum, usually after a cold
OTITIS.rationale: Pain control is always part of care.

SINUSITIS.clue: Facial pain and nasal discharge that persist beyond a typical cold

PHARYNGITIS.clue: Sore throat; group A strep is the one treated to prevent rheumatic fever
PHARYNGITIS.rationale: Cough and runny nose point away from strep.

CROUP.clue: A barking cough and hoarseness from subglottic swelling
CROUP.rationale: Stridor at rest is more serious.

BRONCHIOL.clue: Wheeze and poor feeding in an infant, usually from RSV
BRONCHIOL.rationale: Apnea is a risk in the youngest.

PERTUSSIS.clue: A cough that comes in spasms and ends in a whoop or vomit

INFLUENZA.clue: Sudden fever, ache, and cough in the winter

COVID.clue: A respiratory virus that ranges from a cold to hypoxic pneumonia
COVID.rationale: Prevention is vaccination and isolation when infectious.

ALLERGICRH.clue: Sneezing, itchy eyes, and clear rhinorrhea in a seasonal pattern
ALLERGICRH.rationale: Intranasal steroids are first-line for persistent symptoms.

GLAUCOMA.clue: Optic nerve damage, often with high eye pressure; acute angle closure is an emergency
GLAUCOMA.rationale: Chronic This finding is silent until vision is lost.

CATARACT.clue: Lens clouding that causes glare and slowly worse vision

MACULAR.clue: Central vision loss in older adults from degeneration of the macula

HYPOTHYROID.clue: Fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, and a slow reflex
HYPOTHYROID.rationale: Levothyroxine is taken on an empty stomach.

GRAVES.clue: Autoimmune hyperthyroidism with possible eye disease
GRAVES.rationale: Treatment is drugs, radioiodine, or surgery.

HASHIMOTO.clue: Autoimmune hypothyroidism with a rubbery goiter
HASHIMOTO.rationale: TSH is high and free T4 falls later.

GOITER.clue: An enlarged thyroid, which may be euthyroid, high, or low

DIABETES.clue: High glucose from insulin deficiency or resistance
DIABETES.rationale: Foot checks and kidney screening are part of care.

DKA.clue: High glucose, ketones, and an anion-gap acidosis, usually in type 1
DKA.rationale: Fluids come first, then insulin after potassium is known.

HHS.clue: Extreme glucose and dehydration without major ketones, usually in type 2
HHS.rationale: Fluid replacement is the core treatment.

CUSHING.clue: Central weight, a round face, and high glucose from cortisol excess

ADDISON.clue: Low cortisol with fatigue, low sodium, high potassium, and darker skin
ADDISON.rationale: Crisis is shock treated with steroids and fluids.

PHEOCHROMO.clue: Paroxysms of headache, palpitations, and sweating with high blood pressure
PHEOCHROMO.rationale: Alpha blockade comes before beta blockade.

ACROMEGALY.clue: Enlarging hands, jaw, and shoe size from growth hormone after puberty

SIADH.clue: Low sodium with concentrated urine and no edema
SIADH.rationale: Fluid restriction is first-line when symptoms are mild.

HYPERPARA.clue: High calcium from a parathyroid adenoma, with stones and bone pain
HYPERPARA.rationale: Stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric overtones are the memory line.

RICKETS.clue: Soft growing bone from vitamin D deficiency in children
RICKETS.rationale: Prevention is vitamin D and sun or diet.

SCURVY.clue: Bleeding gums and poor wound healing from vitamin C deficiency
SCURVY.rationale: Vitamin C replacement is the treatment.

BERIBERI.clue: Neuropathy or heart failure from thiamine deficiency

PELLAGRA.clue: Diarrhea, dermatitis, and dementia from niacin deficiency
PELLAGRA.rationale: The fourth D is death if untreated.

KWASHIORKOR.clue: Edema and a fatty liver from protein deficiency with some calories

MARASMUS.clue: Wasting from deficiency of calories and protein

ANEMIA.clue: Low red-cell mass causing fatigue, pallor, and a fast heart rate

IRONDEF.clue: Microcytic anemia from blood loss or poor intake, with low ferritin
IRONDEF.rationale: Do not assume iron deficiency in an older man without looking for blood loss.

FOLATEDEF.clue: Macrocytic anemia without neuropathy, from poor diet or increased demand
FOLATEDEF.rationale: Replace folate, but do not miss B12.

SICKLE.clue: Hemoglobin that polymerizes when oxygen is low, causing pain crises
SICKLE.rationale: Chest pain and fever can be acute chest syndrome.

THALASSEMIA.clue: Inherited reduced globin chains, with microcytosis out of proportion to anemia
THALASSEMIA.rationale: Trait is mild; major is transfusion dependent.

ITP.clue: Low platelets from antibodies, often after a virus in a child

TTP.clue: Low platelets, hemolysis, and neurologic change from ADAMTS13 deficiency

HEMOPHILIA.clue: Deep joint bleeding from a missing clotting factor

VWD.clue: The most common inherited bleeding disorder, with mucosal bleeding

LEUKEMIA.clue: A cancer of white-cell precursors that crowds out normal marrow
LEUKEMIA.rationale: The type is defined by the cell line.

LYMPHOMA.clue: A cancer of lymphoid tissue, with nodes or B symptoms
LYMPHOMA.rationale: Not every enlarged node is This finding.

MYELOMA.clue: A plasma-cell cancer that causes bone pain, anemia, and kidney injury
MYELOMA.rationale: CRAB findings are the memory line.

NEUTROPENIA.clue: A low neutrophil count that makes fever an emergency
NEUTROPENIA.rationale: Do not wait for the source before antibiotics in the unstable.

ALLERGY.clue: An immune response that is harmful, from hay fever to anaphylaxis
ALLERGY.rationale: A rash is not always anaphylaxis, and anaphylaxis is not treated with an antihistamine alone.

ASTHMAEX.clue: An attack that does not respond to the usual rescue doses
ASTHMAEX.rationale: A silent chest is a warning.

COPD.clue: Airflow limitation from emphysema and chronic bronchitis, almost always from smoke
COPD.rationale: Oxygen is titrated; some patients lose their drive if over-oxygenated.

SMOKING.clue: The dominant cause of COPD, lung cancer, and much heart disease

OBESITY.clue: Excess adiposity that drives diabetes, pressure, and joint disease
OBESITY.rationale: Small sustained changes beat crash diets.

PREDIABETES.clue: Glucose above normal but below the diabetes threshold
PREDIABETES.rationale: The label is a chance to act, not a medication mandate for everyone.

METABOLIC.clue: The cluster of central weight, pressure, glucose, and lipids
METABOLIC.rationale: It is a clinic pattern, not one lab.

STATINBEN.clue: The outcome benefit of lowering LDL in patients with vascular risk
STATINBEN.rationale: Benefit is largest in the highest-risk patients.

WARFARIN.clue: Clinical use: oral anticoagulant monitored by INR and reversed with vitamin K
WARFARIN.rationale: This drug blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase. Keep vitamin K intake steady and review CYP2C9 interactions.

HEPARIN.clue: Clinical use: parenteral anticoagulant monitored with aPTT and reversed by protamine
HEPARIN.rationale: Unfractionated This drug potentiates antithrombin. Protamine reverses it; HIT is a platelet-drop emergency.

ENOXAPARIN.clue: Clinical use: weight-based low-molecular-weight heparin with a lower dose when creatinine clearance falls
ENOXAPARIN.rationale: This drug is renally cleared. Anti-Xa monitoring is considered in obesity and kidney disease.

APIXABAN.clue: Clinical use: factor Xa inhibitor that does not require INR monitoring
APIXABAN.rationale: This drug is a direct oral anticoagulant. Dose is reduced for age, weight, and renal function in atrial fibrillation.

RIVAROXABAN.clue: Clinical use: factor Xa inhibitor whose treatment doses are taken with food
RIVAROXABAN.rationale: This drug 15 and 20 mg need food for absorption. Renal function limits use.

DABIGATRAN.clue: Clinical use: direct thrombin inhibitor stored in the original bottle and not crushed
DABIGATRAN.rationale: This drug is moisture sensitive. Bleeding risk rises as renal function falls.

CLOPIDOGREL.clue: Clinical use: p2Y12 antiplatelet prodrug used after coronary stenting
CLOPIDOGREL.rationale: This drug activation depends on CYP2C19. Hold it before elective surgery because of bleeding.

ASPIRIN.clue: Clinical use: irreversible COX inhibitor used for arterial clot prevention
ASPIRIN.rationale: Low-dose This drug inhibits platelet thromboxane for the life of the platelet. Bleeding and ulcer risk remain.

PRASUGREL.clue: Clinical use: potent P2Y12 inhibitor avoided after stroke or TIA
PRASUGREL.rationale: This drug is more potent than clopidogrel and raises bleeding risk, especially in older and low-weight adults.

TICAGRELOR.clue: Clinical use: reversible P2Y12 inhibitor that can cause dyspnea
TICAGRELOR.rationale: This drug is not a prodrug. Doses of aspirin above 100 mg may reduce its benefit.

ALTEPLASE.clue: Clinical use: tissue plasminogen activator used in selected stroke and massive pulmonary embolism
ALTEPLASE.rationale: This drug has a short window and a long list of bleeding exclusions. Blood pressure must be controlled.

PROTAMINE.clue: Clinical use: basic protein that reverses unfractionated heparin
PROTAMINE.rationale: This drug is given slowly. Rapid infusion causes hypotension, and it only partly reverses enoxaparin.

ANDEXANET.clue: Clinical use: reversal agent designed for factor Xa inhibitors
ANDEXANET.rationale: This drug alfa is a decoy factor Xa protein used for life-threatening bleeding on apixaban or rivaroxaban.

LISINOPRIL.clue: Clinical use: aCE inhibitor for hypertension and HFrEF that can raise potassium and cause cough
LISINOPRIL.rationale: This drug is contraindicated in pregnancy and in bilateral renal artery stenosis. Stop it for angioedema.

ENALAPRIL.clue: Clinical use: aCE inhibitor prodrug used in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
ENALAPRIL.rationale: This drug lowers mortality in HFrEF. Monitor creatinine and potassium after starting.

CAPTOPRIL.clue: Clinical use: short-acting ACE inhibitor taken on an empty stomach
CAPTOPRIL.rationale: This drug has a short half-life. Food reduces its absorption, and cough or angioedema means stop the class.

RAMIPRIL.clue: Clinical use: once-daily ACE inhibitor used after myocardial infarction and in high cardiovascular risk
RAMIPRIL.rationale: This drug shares ACE inhibitor risks: hyperkalemia, rising creatinine, cough, and pregnancy contraindication.

LOSARTAN.clue: Clinical use: angiotensin receptor blocker that does not cause the bradykinin cough
LOSARTAN.rationale: This drug blocks AT1 receptors. It is still contraindicated in pregnancy and can raise potassium.

VALSARTAN.clue: Clinical use: aRB used in heart failure and hypertension when an ACE inhibitor is not tolerated
VALSARTAN.rationale: This drug is combined with sacubitril in some heart failure regimens, never with an ACE inhibitor.

SACUBITRIL.clue: Clinical use: neprilysin inhibitor paired with valsartan for HFrEF
SACUBITRIL.rationale: This drug raises natriuretic peptides. A 36-hour washout from an ACE inhibitor is required because of angioedema.

EPLERENONE.clue: Clinical use: selective aldosterone antagonist with less gynecomastia than spironolactone
EPLERENONE.rationale: This drug is a potassium-sparing diuretic used in heart failure and after myocardial infarction.

FUROSEMIDE.clue: Clinical use: loop diuretic for fluid overload that wastes potassium and can injure hearing if pushed fast
FUROSEMIDE.rationale: This drug works even when GFR is low. Watch electrolytes, volume, and ototoxicity with rapid IV doses.

BUMETANIDE.clue: Clinical use: potent loop diuretic used when large furosemide doses are impractical
BUMETANIDE.rationale: This drug is about forty times more potent milligram for milligram than furosemide. Potassium losses are similar.

TORSEMIDE.clue: Clinical use: longer-acting loop diuretic with more reliable oral absorption than furosemide
TORSEMIDE.rationale: This drug is used for edema. Monitor weight, electrolytes, and blood pressure.

HCTZ.clue: Clinical use: thiazide diuretic that can lower potassium and raise uric acid and glucose
HCTZ.rationale: Hydrochlorothiazide is a first-line hypertension option. It is less effective when GFR is very low.

METOLAZONE.clue: Clinical use: thiazide-like diuretic added to a loop for diuretic resistance
METOLAZONE.rationale: This drug is given before the loop dose in sequential nephron blockade. Electrolytes can fall quickly.

METOPROLOL.clue: Clinical use: beta-1 blocker used for heart failure, angina, and rate control
METOPROLOL.rationale: This drug succinate, not the tartrate salt, is the heart-failure evidence formulation. Do not stop abruptly.

CARVEDILOL.clue: Clinical use: nonselective beta blocker with alpha blockade used in HFrEF
CARVEDILOL.rationale: This drug is started low and titrated. It can worsen decompensated fluid overload if begun too soon.

BISOPROLOL.clue: Clinical use: beta-1 selective blocker with a mortality benefit in HFrEF
BISOPROLOL.rationale: This drug is one of the evidence-based beta blockers in systolic heart failure.

ATENOLOL.clue: Clinical use: renally cleared beta blocker that is less used as a first hypertension drug
ATENOLOL.rationale: This drug is cleared by the kidney. It can mask tachycardia from hypoglycemia.

PROPRANOLOL.clue: Clinical use: nonselective beta blocker used for tremor, portal hypertension, and thyroid storm symptoms
PROPRANOLOL.rationale: This drug blocks beta-2 as well, so it can provoke bronchospasm. It is lipophilic and enters the brain.

LABETALOL.clue: Clinical use: combined alpha and beta blocker given IV for hypertensive emergency, including in pregnancy
LABETALOL.rationale: This drug lowers pressure without a pure beta-blocker rise in systemic resistance.

AMLODIPINE.clue: Clinical use: dihydropyridine calcium blocker whose main nuisance effect is ankle edema
AMLODIPINE.rationale: This drug dilates arteries. The edema is from precapillary vasodilation, not heart failure by itself.

NIFEDIPINE.clue: Clinical use: dihydropyridine used for hypertension; immediate-release capsules are avoided for emergencies
NIFEDIPINE.rationale: Immediate-release This drug can cause reflex tachycardia and ischemia. Extended release is the outpatient form.

DILTIAZEM.clue: Clinical use: non-dihydropyridine calcium blocker used for rate control that is avoided in HFrEF
DILTIAZEM.rationale: This drug slows the AV node. It is a CYP3A4 inhibitor and can worsen systolic heart failure.

VERAPAMIL.clue: Clinical use: calcium blocker that slows heart rate and commonly causes constipation
VERAPAMIL.rationale: This drug is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor. Avoid it with HFrEF and with many simvastatin doses.

DIGOXIN.clue: Clinical use: cardiac glycoside for rate control and symptoms whose toxicity rises when potassium is low
DIGOXIN.rationale: This drug is renally cleared. Nausea, visual changes, and arrhythmias suggest toxicity.

AMIODARONE.clue: Clinical use: iodine-containing antiarrhythmic that can injure lung, thyroid, and liver
AMIODARONE.rationale: This drug has a half-life of many weeks. It inhibits warfarin metabolism and raises digoxin levels.

SOTALOL.clue: Clinical use: antiarrhythmic beta blocker that prolongs the QT and is started with monitoring
SOTALOL.rationale: This drug is renally cleared. QT prolongation and torsades are the initiation risk.

DOFETILIDE.clue: Clinical use: class III antiarrhythmic started in a monitored setting because of torsades
DOFETILIDE.rationale: This drug dose depends on kidney function and the QT interval. Many drugs are contraindicated with it.

FLECAINIDE.clue: Clinical use: class Ic antiarrhythmic avoided in structural heart disease
FLECAINIDE.rationale: This drug can be used for atrial fibrillation in a normal heart. It is proarrhythmic after myocardial infarction.

ADENOSINE.clue: Clinical use: very short-acting drug given as a rapid push for stable SVT
ADENOSINE.rationale: This drug briefly blocks the AV node. Warn the patient about chest discomfort and a pause.

ATROPINE.clue: Clinical use: antimuscarinic first drug for symptomatic bradycardia
ATROPINE.rationale: This drug raises heart rate by blocking vagal tone. It does not help a denervated transplanted heart.

DOPAMINE.clue: Clinical use: dose-dependent vasopressor and inotrope
DOPAMINE.rationale: Low This drug doses are not renal-protective. Higher doses raise heart rate and vasoconstriction.

DOBUTAMINE.clue: Clinical use: beta-1 inotrope used in cardiogenic shock
DOBUTAMINE.rationale: This drug increases contractility and can provoke ischemia or arrhythmias.

MILRINONE.clue: Clinical use: pDE-3 inhibitor that is an inotrope and vasodilator
MILRINONE.rationale: This drug is renally cleared and causes hypotension. It is used in advanced heart failure.

VASOPRESSIN.clue: Clinical use: non-catecholamine vasopressor also used to replace ADH
VASOPRESSIN.rationale: This drug is added in vasodilatory shock and treats central diabetes insipidus.

HYDRALAZINE.clue: Clinical use: arterial vasodilator that causes reflex tachycardia and a lupus-like syndrome
HYDRALAZINE.rationale: This drug is often paired with a nitrate in heart failure when ACE inhibitors cannot be used.

ISOSORBIDE.clue: Clinical use: nitrate used for angina and heart failure that requires a nitrate-free interval
ISOSORBIDE.rationale: This drug tolerance develops without a daily drug-free interval. It is contraindicated with PDE-5 inhibitors.

SILDENAFIL.clue: Clinical use: pDE-5 inhibitor that is dangerous with nitrates
SILDENAFIL.rationale: This drug is used for erectile dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension. Nitrates are contraindicated.

TADALAFIL.clue: Clinical use: long-acting PDE-5 inhibitor also used for pulmonary hypertension and urinary symptoms
TADALAFIL.rationale: This drug lasts longer than sildenafil. The nitrate interaction window is longer too.

SIMVASTATIN.clue: Clinical use: statin with a dose cap when combined with amlodipine or certain CYP3A4 inhibitors
SIMVASTATIN.rationale: This drug myopathy risk rises with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. High doses are restricted.

PRAVASTATIN.clue: Clinical use: statin not metabolized by CYP3A4, useful when interactions are a concern
PRAVASTATIN.rationale: This drug is hydrophilic and has fewer CYP drug interactions than simvastatin.

EZETIMIBE.clue: Clinical use: cholesterol absorption inhibitor added when statin LDL lowering is not enough
EZETIMIBE.rationale: This drug blocks intestinal cholesterol uptake. It is often combined with a statin.

FENOFIBRATE.clue: Clinical use: fibrate that lowers triglycerides and is preferred over gemfibrozil with a statin
FENOFIBRATE.rationale: This drug has less statin interaction than gemfibrozil, but muscle risk is not zero.

GEMFIBROZIL.clue: Clinical use: fibrate that should not be combined with simvastatin because of rhabdomyolysis
GEMFIBROZIL.rationale: This drug inhibits statin glucuronidation. The combination with simvastatin is contraindicated.

NIACIN.clue: Clinical use: lipid drug that causes flushing, which can be reduced by taking aspirin before it
NIACIN.rationale: This drug raises HDL and can worsen glucose and uric acid. Flushing is prostaglandin mediated.

COLESEVELAM.clue: Clinical use: bile acid sequestrant that lowers LDL and can bind other oral drugs
COLESEVELAM.rationale: This drug is taken with meals and separated from other medications. It can raise triglycerides.

METFORMIN.clue: Clinical use: first-line biguanide for type 2 diabetes that is held around iodinated contrast
METFORMIN.rationale: This drug does not cause hypoglycemia alone. Lactic acidosis risk rises when the kidneys cannot clear it.

GLIPIZIDE.clue: Clinical use: sulfonylurea that releases insulin and can cause hypoglycemia
GLIPIZIDE.rationale: This drug must be taken with food. Skip the dose if the patient is not eating.

GLYBURIDE.clue: Clinical use: long-acting sulfonylurea generally avoided in older adults
GLYBURIDE.rationale: This drug causes prolonged hypoglycemia and is on beers-criteria avoidance lists.

GLIMEPIRIDE.clue: Clinical use: sulfonylurea taken once daily that still carries hypoglycemia risk
GLIMEPIRIDE.rationale: This drug stimulates insulin release. Renal impairment prolongs the effect.

REPAGLINIDE.clue: Clinical use: meglitinide taken with meals that is skipped when a meal is skipped
REPAGLINIDE.rationale: This drug has a short action. Gemfibrozil is contraindicated because it markedly raises levels.

SITAGLIPTIN.clue: Clinical use: dPP-4 inhibitor that is weight neutral and rarely causes hypoglycemia alone
SITAGLIPTIN.rationale: This drug dose is reduced in kidney disease. Pancreatitis is a rare warning.

LINAGLIPTIN.clue: Clinical use: dPP-4 inhibitor that does not need renal dose adjustment
LINAGLIPTIN.rationale: This drug is excreted by the bile. It is an option when creatinine clearance is low.

LIRAGLUTIDE.clue: Clinical use: daily GLP-1 agonist that helps weight and has a boxed thyroid C-cell warning
LIRAGLUTIDE.rationale: This drug slows gastric emptying. Nausea is common and pancreatitis is a stop-the-drug symptom.

SEMAGLUTIDE.clue: Clinical use: gLP-1 agonist available as a weekly injection or an oral tablet taken on an empty stomach
SEMAGLUTIDE.rationale: Oral This drug is taken with a small sip of water and no food for 30 minutes. GI effects are common.

INSULIN.clue: Clinical use: hormone replacement that causes hypoglycemia and is a high-alert medication
INSULIN.rationale: This drug doses are double-checked. Rotate sites and match mealtime This drug to carbohydrate intake.

LISPRO.clue: Clinical use: rapid-acting insulin given with the meal, not long before the tray arrives
LISPRO.rationale: This drug starts within minutes. Giving it and delaying food causes hypoglycemia.

GLARGINE.clue: Clinical use: long-acting insulin with no pronounced peak that is not mixed in the same syringe
GLARGINE.rationale: Insulin This drug is usually once daily. Do not mix it with other insulins.

DETEMIR.clue: Clinical use: long-acting insulin bound to albumin, dosed once or twice daily
DETEMIR.rationale: Insulin This drug has a relatively flat profile. It is not mixed with other insulins.

NPH.clue: Clinical use: cloudy intermediate insulin with a peak that requires a planned snack or meal
NPH.rationale: This drug is rolled, not shaken. When mixing, it is drawn after the clear short-acting insulin.

METHIMAZOLE.clue: Clinical use: antithyroid drug avoided in the first trimester because of teratogenicity
METHIMAZOLE.rationale: This drug can cause agranulocytosis. Fever or sore throat means stop the drug and check a white count.

PREDNISONE.clue: Clinical use: corticosteroid that must be tapered after long courses and raises glucose
PREDNISONE.rationale: This drug causes infection risk, insomnia, and adrenal suppression. Do not stop a long course abruptly.

ALENDRONATE.clue: Clinical use: bisphosphonate taken weekly with a full glass of water, staying upright
ALENDRONATE.rationale: This drug can cause esophagitis. Separate it from food, calcium, and other drugs by at least 30 minutes.

RISEDRONATE.clue: Clinical use: oral bisphosphonate for osteoporosis with the same upright dosing rules
RISEDRONATE.rationale: This drug inhibits osteoclasts. Dental exams matter because of rare osteonecrosis of the jaw.

ZOLEDRONIC.clue: Clinical use: yearly IV bisphosphonate that requires adequate hydration and a normal calcium
ZOLEDRONIC.rationale: This drug acid can cause an acute phase reaction. Check creatinine and calcium before each dose.

DENOSUMAB.clue: Clinical use: rANKL inhibitor given every six months that can cause hypocalcemia
DENOSUMAB.rationale: This drug is not a bisphosphonate. Stopping it without a follow-on drug can cause rebound fractures.

RALOXIFENE.clue: Clinical use: sERM that reduces vertebral fractures and raises clot risk
RALOXIFENE.rationale: This drug is an estrogen agonist in bone and an antagonist in breast. It can cause hot flashes and VTE.

CALCITONIN.clue: Clinical use: nasal or injectable hormone sometimes used for acute pain of vertebral fracture
CALCITONIN.rationale: This drug has a small fracture benefit. Nasal irritation is a common effect.

CALCIUM.clue: Clinical use: mineral supplement separated from levothyroxine, quinolones, and tetracyclines
CALCIUM.rationale: This drug binds many drugs in the gut. Citrate is the form that does not need stomach acid.

VITAMIND.clue: Clinical use: supplement needed for calcium absorption and often low in osteoporosis
VITAMIND.rationale: Vitamin D deficiency is corrected before judging a calcium or bisphosphonate plan. Toxicity causes hypercalcemia.

FERROUS.clue: Clinical use: oral iron that causes dark stools and constipation and is best on an empty stomach
FERROUS.rationale: This drug sulfate absorption falls with food, antacids, and tea. Vitamin C juice can help absorption.

FOLICACID.clue: Clinical use: vitamin given before conception and with methotrexate rescue plans in some protocols
FOLICACID.rationale: Folic acid prevents neural tube defects. In methotrexate therapy, folate timing follows the protocol so efficacy is preserved.

PYRIDOXINE.clue: Clinical use: vitamin B6 given with isoniazid to prevent neuropathy
PYRIDOXINE.rationale: This drug is also used for isoniazid overdose seizures. Routine high doses can themselves cause neuropathy.

THIAMINE.clue: Clinical use: vitamin given before glucose in malnourished patients to prevent Wernicke injury
THIAMINE.rationale: This drug deficiency causes confusion, ataxia, and eye-movement palsy. Replace it in alcohol withdrawal protocols.

POTASSIUM.clue: Clinical use: electrolyte replacement never given as an IV push
POTASSIUM.rationale: Oral This drug is preferred when the gut works. IV This drug is diluted and infused slowly.

MAGNESIUM.clue: Clinical use: electrolyte replaced when potassium will not stay corrected, and the antidote for torsades
MAGNESIUM.rationale: Hypomagnesemia causes refractory hypokalemia. IV This drug treats torsades de pointes.

PHOSPHATE.clue: Clinical use: electrolyte that falls in refeeding and binds oral calcium
PHOSPHATE.rationale: This drug replacement is oral when possible. IV This drug can cause hypocalcemia if given too fast.

SEVELAMER.clue: Clinical use: non-calcium phosphate binder taken with meals in chronic kidney disease
SEVELAMER.rationale: This drug binds dietary phosphate. It does not add to the calcium load the way calcium binders do.

KAYEXALATE.clue: Clinical use: sodium polystyrene resin that removes potassium slowly through the gut
KAYEXALATE.rationale: This resin is not the emergency treatment for ECG changes from hyperkalemia. It can cause intestinal injury.

PATIROMER.clue: Clinical use: potassium binder taken with food and separated from other oral drugs
PATIROMER.rationale: This drug exchanges calcium for potassium in the gut. Separate other medications by several hours.

EPOETIN.clue: Clinical use: erythropoiesis-stimulating agent that raises clot and blood pressure risk if hemoglobin is pushed high
EPOETIN.rationale: This drug is used for anemia of chronic kidney disease. Target hemoglobin is not normalized.

AMOXICILLIN.clue: Clinical use: aminopenicillin for otitis, sinusitis, and strep throat
AMOXICILLIN.rationale: This drug is a beta-lactam. A rash during mono is common and is not always a true allergy.

AMPICILLIN.clue: Clinical use: aminopenicillin used for enterococcal infection and some meningitis regimens
AMPICILLIN.rationale: This drug covers susceptible enterococci. A high IV dose is used when meningitis coverage is intended.

PENICILLIN.clue: Clinical use: beta-lactam of choice for syphilis and many streptococcal infections
PENICILLIN.rationale: This drug G remains the treatment for syphilis. Allergy history decides whether a cephalosporin is reasonable.

NAFCILLIN.clue: Clinical use: antistaphylococcal penicillin cleared by the liver, used for serious MSSA
NAFCILLIN.rationale: This drug does not need renal adjustment. It can cause interstitial nephritis.

OXACILLIN.clue: Clinical use: penicillinase-resistant penicillin for methicillin-sensitive staph
OXACILLIN.rationale: This drug is used for MSSA. It does not cover MRSA or enterococci.

CEFAZOLIN.clue: Clinical use: first-generation cephalosporin used for surgical prophylaxis
CEFAZOLIN.rationale: This drug covers skin flora including MSSA. It is the usual pre-incision antibiotic.

CEPHALEXIN.clue: Clinical use: oral first-generation cephalosporin for skin and urinary infections
CEPHALEXIN.rationale: This drug is taken several times a day. It does not cover MRSA.

CEFTRIAXONE.clue: Clinical use: third-generation cephalosporin for meningitis, gonorrhea, and serious gram-negative infection
CEFTRIAXONE.rationale: This drug reaches the CSF. It can sludge the gallbladder and is avoided with calcium-containing IV fluids in neonates.

CEFEPIME.clue: Clinical use: fourth-generation cephalosporin with pseudomonas coverage
CEFEPIME.rationale: This drug can cause neurotoxicity when the dose is not reduced for kidney function.

CEFTAZIDIME.clue: Clinical use: third-generation cephalosporin used when pseudomonas coverage is needed
CEFTAZIDIME.rationale: This drug lacks reliable gram-positive coverage. It is a pseudomonas cephalosporin.

MEROPENEM.clue: Clinical use: carbapenem for resistant infection that can lower the seizure threshold
MEROPENEM.rationale: This drug covers anaerobes and many resistant gram-negatives. Dose is reduced in renal failure.

IMIPENEM.clue: Clinical use: carbapenem given with cilastatin and known for seizure risk
IMIPENEM.rationale: This drug is paired with cilastatin to block renal breakdown. Seizure risk is higher than with meropenem.

ERTAPENEM.clue: Clinical use: once-daily carbapenem that does not cover pseudomonas or acinetobacter
ERTAPENEM.rationale: This drug is convenient but is the wrong carbapenem when pseudomonas is a concern.

AZTREONAM.clue: Clinical use: monobactam safe in most penicillin allergies, covering aerobic gram-negatives
AZTREONAM.rationale: This drug has no gram-positive or anaerobic activity. It can be used when a beta-lactam allergy is severe.

VANCOMYCIN.clue: Clinical use: glycopeptide for MRSA that is infused slowly to avoid flushing
VANCOMYCIN.rationale: This drug flushing is rate related. Trough or AUC monitoring limits kidney injury.

DAPTOMYCIN.clue: Clinical use: lipopeptide for resistant gram-positive infection that is inactivated by lung surfactant
DAPTOMYCIN.rationale: This drug is not used for pneumonia. It can raise CPK, so muscle symptoms are reported.

LINEZOLID.clue: Clinical use: oxazolidinone for MRSA and VRE that can cause serotonin syndrome
LINEZOLID.rationale: This drug is a weak MAO inhibitor. Thrombocytopenia rises with courses longer than two weeks.

GENTAMICIN.clue: Clinical use: aminoglycoside monitored for kidney and ear toxicity with peaks and troughs
GENTAMICIN.rationale: This drug is often once daily for synergy or traditional dosing. Troughs that stay high predict toxicity.

TOBRAMYCIN.clue: Clinical use: aminoglycoside often chosen for pseudomonas, with the same toxicity profile
TOBRAMYCIN.rationale: This drug needs renal dosing and hearing checks on long courses. It is given with a cell-wall agent for synergy.

AMIKACIN.clue: Clinical use: aminoglycoside reserved for more resistant gram-negative organisms
AMIKACIN.rationale: This drug is dosed by kidney function. It shares ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity with the class.

DOXYCYCLINE.clue: Clinical use: tetracycline for Lyme disease, acne, and atypical pneumonia that stains teeth
DOXYCYCLINE.rationale: This drug is avoided in pregnancy and young children. Separate it from iron, calcium, and antacids.

MINOCYCLINE.clue: Clinical use: tetracycline used for acne that can cause vestibular symptoms and blue-gray skin
MINOCYCLINE.rationale: This drug is separated from divalent cations. Drug-induced lupus is a rare effect.

CLINDAMYCIN.clue: Clinical use: lincosamide with anaerobic coverage and a high risk of C. difficile
CLINDAMYCIN.rationale: This drug diarrhea is assumed to be C. difficile until proven otherwise. It also covers some MRSA skin infection.

TINIDAZOLE.clue: Clinical use: nitroimidazole for trichomonas, giardia, and some anaerobic infections
TINIDAZOLE.rationale: This drug has a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, similar to metronidazole.

FOSFOMYCIN.clue: Clinical use: single-dose oral antibiotic for uncomplicated cystitis
FOSFOMYCIN.rationale: This drug is mixed in water and taken once. It is not the drug for pyelonephritis.

FLUCONAZOLE.clue: Clinical use: azole antifungal for candida that inhibits CYP enzymes
FLUCONAZOLE.rationale: This drug raises levels of warfarin, some statins, and phenytoin. A one-time dose treats uncomplicated vaginal candida.

CASPOFUNGIN.clue: Clinical use: echinocandin for invasive candida that is not absorbed orally
CASPOFUNGIN.rationale: This drug is IV only. It is preferred for unstable candidemia over fluconazole.

MICAFUNGIN.clue: Clinical use: echinocandin alternative for candidemia with few drug interactions
MICAFUNGIN.rationale: This drug covers candida species including many fluconazole-resistant isolates. It does not treat cryptococcus.

NYSTATIN.clue: Clinical use: topical or swish antifungal for thrush that is not systemically absorbed
NYSTATIN.rationale: This drug suspension is swished and swallowed. It will not treat invasive fungal disease.

TERBINAFINE.clue: Clinical use: oral antifungal for nail dermatophyte infection that can injure the liver
TERBINAFINE.rationale: This drug is taken for weeks for onychomycosis. Check the liver and watch for taste change.

ACYCLOVIR.clue: Clinical use: antiviral for herpes that needs hydration to protect the kidneys
ACYCLOVIR.rationale: This drug crystals can obstruct tubules. Oral doses are adjusted for creatinine clearance.

GANCICLOVIR.clue: Clinical use: antiviral for cytomegalovirus that causes bone marrow suppression
GANCICLOVIR.rationale: This drug is handled as a hazardous drug. Neutropenia is the limiting toxicity.

FAMCICLOVIR.clue: Clinical use: oral prodrug of penciclovir used for herpes zoster and recurrent genital herpes
FAMCICLOVIR.rationale: This drug is started early in a zoster outbreak. Dose is reduced in kidney disease.

OSELTAMIVIR.clue: Clinical use: neuraminidase inhibitor most useful within 48 hours of influenza onset
OSELTAMIVIR.rationale: This drug shortens flu illness. Neuropsychiatric effects are reported, and the dose is renal.

ZANAMIVIR.clue: Clinical use: inhaled neuraminidase inhibitor avoided in asthma and COPD
ZANAMIVIR.rationale: This drug can cause bronchospasm. It is not the flu drug for a patient who cannot inhale a powder.

BALOXAVIR.clue: Clinical use: single-dose endonuclease inhibitor for influenza
BALOXAVIR.rationale: This drug is one dose. It is not combined casually with polyvalent cations, which bind it.

RIBAVIRIN.clue: Clinical use: antiviral used in some hepatitis C regimens that is teratogenic
RIBAVIRIN.rationale: This drug requires two forms of contraception during and after therapy because of birth defects.

SOFOSBUVIR.clue: Clinical use: nS5B inhibitor used in hepatitis C combinations
SOFOSBUVIR.rationale: This drug is the backbone of several hepatitis C regimens. Amiodarone with it can cause severe bradycardia.

TENOFOVIR.clue: Clinical use: nucleotide analog for HIV and hepatitis B that can injure kidneys and bone
TENOFOVIR.rationale: This drug disoproxil is the salt linked with Fanconi syndrome. The alafenamide salt has less kidney and bone toxicity.

LAMIVUDINE.clue: Clinical use: cytosine analog for HIV and hepatitis B with a low barrier if used alone for hepatitis B
LAMIVUDINE.rationale: This drug monotherapy for hepatitis B selects resistance. It is well tolerated.

ABACAVIR.clue: Clinical use: nucleoside analog that requires HLA-B5701 screening because of hypersensitivity
ABACAVIR.rationale: Never rechallenge This drug after a hypersensitivity reaction. The reaction can include fever, rash, and respiratory symptoms.

RALTEGRAVIR.clue: Clinical use: integrase inhibitor for HIV with few drug interactions
RALTEGRAVIR.rationale: This drug can raise CPK. It is taken with or without food depending on the formulation.

EFAVIRENZ.clue: Clinical use: nNRTI that causes vivid dreams and is taken on an empty stomach at bedtime
EFAVIRENZ.rationale: This drug is teratogenic in animal data and is CNS active. Food increases levels and side effects.

RITONAVIR.clue: Clinical use: strong CYP3A4 inhibitor used as a pharmacokinetic booster
RITONAVIR.rationale: This drug raises levels of many drugs. Review the whole medication list before it is added.

COBICISTAT.clue: Clinical use: pharmacokinetic booster that inhibits CYP3A4 and raises creatinine slightly
COBICISTAT.rationale: This drug blocks tubular creatinine secretion, so the creatinine bump is not always a GFR drop.

ATAZANAVIR.clue: Clinical use: protease inhibitor that needs an acid stomach and can cause jaundice
ATAZANAVIR.rationale: This drug is not combined with proton pump inhibitors in treatment-experienced patients. Indirect bilirubin rises.

DARUNAVIR.clue: Clinical use: protease inhibitor boosted with ritonavir or cobicistat and used with a sulfa caution
DARUNAVIR.rationale: This drug contains a sulfa moiety. Rash is possible in sulfa-allergic patients, and it is taken with food.

ISONIAZID.clue: Clinical use: tuberculosis drug that causes neuropathy unless pyridoxine is given
ISONIAZID.rationale: This drug is hepatotoxic and depletes vitamin B6. A positive hepatitis symptom means stop and check enzymes.

RIFAMPIN.clue: Clinical use: potent CYP inducer used for tuberculosis that turns body fluids orange
RIFAMPIN.rationale: This drug lowers levels of warfarin, oral contraceptives, and many antiretrovirals. Counsel about orange urine.

RIFABUTIN.clue: Clinical use: rifamycin with fewer CYP interactions, used when rifampin cannot be combined
RIFABUTIN.rationale: This drug still induces enzymes, but less than rifampin. Uveitis is a toxicity.

ETHAMBUTOL.clue: Clinical use: tuberculosis drug that can cause optic neuritis
ETHAMBUTOL.rationale: This drug toxicity is color-vision loss. Baseline and periodic eye exams are part of safe use.

BEDAQUILINE.clue: Clinical use: drug for resistant tuberculosis that prolongs the QT interval
BEDAQUILINE.rationale: This drug is used in multidrug-resistant tuberculosis regimens. ECG monitoring is required.

DAPSONE.clue: Clinical use: drug for leprosy and pneumocystis prevention that causes hemolysis in G6PD deficiency
DAPSONE.rationale: This drug is oxidant stress. Screen for G6PD deficiency before use when possible.

ATOVAQUONE.clue: Clinical use: drug for pneumocystis and with proguanil for malaria, taken with food
ATOVAQUONE.rationale: This drug absorption needs dietary fat. It is an option when trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole cannot be used.

PRIMAQUINE.clue: Clinical use: antimalarial that eradicates liver stages and causes hemolysis in G6PD deficiency
PRIMAQUINE.rationale: This drug is the hypnozoite drug for vivax and ovale. Test G6PD before the first dose.

CHLOROQUINE.clue: Clinical use: antimalarial that can cause retinal toxicity with long use
CHLOROQUINE.rationale: This drug is also used in some autoimmune disease. Eye exams are required for chronic therapy.

QUININE.clue: Clinical use: antimalarial that causes cinchonism: tinnitus, headache, and visual change
QUININE.rationale: This drug is not a casual leg-cramp drug. It prolongs the QT and causes hypoglycemia.

ARTESUNATE.clue: Clinical use: iV artemisinin used for severe malaria
ARTESUNATE.rationale: This drug is the preferred parenteral treatment for severe malaria. Delayed hemolysis can follow treatment.

ALBENDAZOLE.clue: Clinical use: anthelmintic taken with a fatty meal for tissue parasites
ALBENDAZOLE.rationale: This drug is used for neurocysticercosis and some worm infections. Liver enzymes are checked on long courses.

IVERMECTIN.clue: Clinical use: antiparasitic for strongyloides and onchocerciasis, taken on an empty stomach
IVERMECTIN.rationale: This drug does not kill adult onchocerca immediately. Mazzotti reactions can follow treatment of onchocerciasis.

PERMETHRIN.clue: Clinical use: topical scabicide applied from neck to toes and washed off after the labeled time
PERMETHRIN.rationale: This drug 5 percent is the usual scabies treatment. Household contacts are treated at the same time.

SERTRALINE.clue: Clinical use: sSRI with fewer CYP interactions than fluoxetine or paroxetine
SERTRALINE.rationale: This drug takes weeks for mood. Combining it with MAO inhibitors or linezolid risks serotonin syndrome.

FLUOXETINE.clue: Clinical use: long half-life SSRI that inhibits CYP2D6
FLUOXETINE.rationale: This drug and its metabolite linger for weeks. A long washout is needed before an MAO inhibitor.

PAROXETINE.clue: Clinical use: sSRI most associated with withdrawal symptoms and CYP2D6 inhibition
PAROXETINE.rationale: This drug is more anticholinergic than other SSRIs and is avoided in pregnancy when possible.

CITALOPRAM.clue: Clinical use: sSRI with a dose cap because of QT prolongation
CITALOPRAM.rationale: This drug doses above 40 mg are avoided, and above 20 mg in older adults, because of the QT risk.

VENLAFAXINE.clue: Clinical use: sNRI that can raise blood pressure as the dose increases
VENLAFAXINE.rationale: This drug withdrawal is uncomfortable if it is stopped suddenly. Check blood pressure at higher doses.

DULOXETINE.clue: Clinical use: sNRI used for depression and neuropathic or musculoskeletal pain
DULOXETINE.rationale: This drug is avoided in substantial liver disease and in severe kidney disease. It can raise blood pressure.

BUPROPION.clue: Clinical use: antidepressant that lowers the seizure threshold and helps with smoking cessation
BUPROPION.rationale: This drug is avoided in bulimia, anorexia, and seizure disorders. It does not cause SSRI sexual side effects.

MIRTAZAPINE.clue: Clinical use: antidepressant that causes sedation and increased appetite
MIRTAZAPINE.rationale: This drug is useful when insomnia and poor appetite are problems. Weight gain is expected.

TRAZODONE.clue: Clinical use: sedating antidepressant used for sleep that can cause priapism
TRAZODONE.rationale: This drug is not a benzodiazepine. A prolonged erection is an emergency.

DOXEPIN.clue: Clinical use: tricyclic used in low doses for sleep and itching, with anticholinergic effects at higher doses
DOXEPIN.rationale: This drug in depression doses prolongs the QT and is dangerous in overdose. Low doses are for insomnia.

IMIPRAMINE.clue: Clinical use: tricyclic antidepressant with anticholinergic effects and cardiac toxicity in overdose
IMIPRAMINE.rationale: This drug overdose causes seizures and wide-complex arrhythmias. It is not a first-line antidepressant.

PHENELZINE.clue: Clinical use: irreversible MAO inhibitor that requires a low-tyramine diet
PHENELZINE.rationale: This drug plus an SSRI, meperidine, or dextromethorphan can cause serotonin syndrome or a hypertensive crisis.

SELEGILINE.clue: Clinical use: mAO-B inhibitor for Parkinson disease; the patch can lose selectivity
SELEGILINE.rationale: Dietary tyramine restrictions apply to higher-dose This drug patch, not always to low oral MAO-B doses.

HALOPERIDOL.clue: Clinical use: first-generation antipsychotic that causes dystonia and QT prolongation
HALOPERIDOL.rationale: This drug is not used IV without caution because of the QT. Acute dystonia is treated with an anticholinergic.

RISPERIDONE.clue: Clinical use: atypical antipsychotic with a relatively high risk of prolactin elevation and EPS
RISPERIDONE.rationale: This drug causes hyperprolactinemia. Dose-related extrapyramidal symptoms are more common than with quetiapine.

OLANZAPINE.clue: Clinical use: atypical antipsychotic with marked weight gain and metabolic effects
OLANZAPINE.rationale: This drug is sedating and anticholinergic. Smoking induces its clearance.

QUETIAPINE.clue: Clinical use: atypical antipsychotic often used for sedation, with metabolic risk and a low EPS risk
QUETIAPINE.rationale: This drug is sometimes misused for sleep. It still causes weight gain and QT effects.

ZIPRASIDONE.clue: Clinical use: atypical antipsychotic that must be taken with food and prolongs the QT
ZIPRASIDONE.rationale: This drug absorption doubles with a meal of adequate calories. It is avoided when the QT is already long.

LURASIDONE.clue: Clinical use: atypical antipsychotic taken with food that has less metabolic effect than olanzapine
LURASIDONE.rationale: This drug is taken with at least 350 calories. It is a CYP3A4 substrate.

CLOZAPINE.clue: Clinical use: most effective antipsychotic, reserved for treatment resistance because of agranulocytosis
CLOZAPINE.rationale: This drug requires absolute neutrophil count monitoring. Constipation, sialorrhea, and myocarditis are other risks.

LITHIUM.clue: Clinical use: mood stabilizer with a narrow therapeutic index that rises when sodium is lost
LITHIUM.rationale: This drug toxicity follows dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, and thiazides. Tremor and confusion are early signs.

VALPROATE.clue: Clinical use: mood stabilizer and antiseizure drug that is teratogenic and hepatotoxic
VALPROATE.rationale: This drug is avoided in pregnancy. Ammonia is checked if cognition changes, and platelets can fall.

LAMOTRIGINE.clue: Clinical use: antiseizure and mood drug titrated slowly because of Stevens-Johnson risk
LAMOTRIGINE.rationale: Valproate doubles This drug levels, so the titration is slower. Any rash stops the drug.

LORAZEPAM.clue: Clinical use: benzodiazepine preferred in liver disease because it is glucuronidated
LORAZEPAM.rationale: This drug is used for status epilepticus and alcohol withdrawal. It depresses breathing with opioids.

DIAZEPAM.clue: Clinical use: long-acting benzodiazepine for seizures, spasms, and alcohol withdrawal
DIAZEPAM.rationale: This drug has active metabolites. It accumulates in older adults and in liver disease.

ALPRAZOLAM.clue: Clinical use: short-acting benzodiazepine with a difficult withdrawal
ALPRAZOLAM.rationale: This drug is tapered. Abrupt cessation can cause rebound anxiety and seizures.

CLONAZEPAM.clue: Clinical use: long-acting benzodiazepine used for panic and some seizure types
CLONAZEPAM.rationale: This drug lasts longer than alprazolam. Sedation and dependence are the counseling points.

MIDAZOLAM.clue: Clinical use: short-acting benzodiazepine used for procedural sedation
MIDAZOLAM.rationale: This drug is reversed with flumazenil only when the airway is protected and chronic use is unlikely.

FLUMAZENIL.clue: Clinical use: benzodiazepine antagonist that can precipitate seizures
FLUMAZENIL.rationale: This drug is avoided in chronic benzodiazepine use and in mixed overdoses with proconvulsant drugs.

ZOLPIDEM.clue: Clinical use: non-benzodiazepine hypnotic with complex sleep behaviors
ZOLPIDEM.rationale: This drug is taken only when ready for bed. Lower doses are used in women and older adults.

ESZOPICLONE.clue: Clinical use: hypnotic that can leave a metallic taste
ESZOPICLONE.rationale: This drug is a controlled sleep drug. Next-day impairment is possible.

BUSPIRONE.clue: Clinical use: non-sedating anxiolytic that takes weeks and has no cross-tolerance with benzodiazepines
BUSPIRONE.rationale: This drug is not a rescue drug for a panic attack. It is a scheduled anxiolytic.

AMPHETAMINE.clue: Clinical use: stimulant for ADHD that raises heart rate and blood pressure and suppresses appetite
AMPHETAMINE.rationale: Amphetamines are controlled substances. They are avoided in structural heart disease and uncontrolled hypertension.

ATOMOXETINE.clue: Clinical use: non-stimulant ADHD drug that is a CYP2D6 substrate and carries a suicidal-ideation warning
ATOMOXETINE.rationale: This drug takes weeks. It can raise blood pressure and is not a controlled stimulant.

GUANFACINE.clue: Clinical use: alpha-2 agonist for ADHD that is not stopped abruptly
GUANFACINE.rationale: This drug extended release can cause hypotension and rebound hypertension if stopped suddenly.

CLONIDINE.clue: Clinical use: central alpha agonist whose sudden stop causes rebound hypertension
CLONIDINE.rationale: This drug patches are replaced on schedule. The oral drug is tapered.

DONEPEZIL.clue: Clinical use: cholinesterase inhibitor for Alzheimer disease that causes GI upset and bradycardia
DONEPEZIL.rationale: This drug increases acetylcholine. Diarrhea, vivid dreams, and a slow heart rate are expected effects.

GALANTAMINE.clue: Clinical use: cholinesterase inhibitor taken with food that needs renal and hepatic dose limits
GALANTAMINE.rationale: This drug shares the cholinergic side effects of donepezil. Dose is reduced when clearance is low.

MEMANTINE.clue: Clinical use: nMDA antagonist for moderate Alzheimer disease that is renally dosed
MEMANTINE.rationale: This drug is often added to a cholinesterase inhibitor. Dizziness and confusion can occur.

CARBIDOPA.clue: Clinical use: decarboxylase inhibitor that lets more levodopa reach the brain
CARBIDOPA.rationale: This drug reduces peripheral nausea from levodopa. It does not treat Parkinson disease by itself.

LEVODOPA.clue: Clinical use: dopamine precursor for Parkinson disease that causes dyskinesias over time
LEVODOPA.rationale: This drug is the most effective motor drug. Protein meals can compete with its absorption.

ENTACAPONE.clue: Clinical use: cOMT inhibitor that extends levodopa effect and can darken urine
ENTACAPONE.rationale: This drug is only useful with levodopa. Diarrhea and brown-orange urine are counseling points.

PRAMIPEXOLE.clue: Clinical use: dopamine agonist that can cause sudden sleep and impulse-control problems
PRAMIPEXOLE.rationale: This drug is renally cleared. Warn about gambling, hypersexuality, and falling asleep while driving.

ROPINIROLE.clue: Clinical use: dopamine agonist also used for restless legs
ROPINIROLE.rationale: This drug is metabolized by CYP1A2. Smoking changes its levels, and impulse-control disorders occur.

BENZTROPINE.clue: Clinical use: anticholinergic for drug-induced parkinsonism and dystonia
BENZTROPINE.rationale: This drug is avoided in older adults because of confusion, retention, and constipation.

MORPHINE.clue: Clinical use: full opioid agonist that releases histamine and is renally cleared to an active metabolite
MORPHINE.rationale: This drug causes constipation, which is prevented, not waited for. Active metabolites accumulate in kidney failure.

OXYCODONE.clue: Clinical use: oral opioid available alone or with acetaminophen
OXYCODONE.rationale: This drug combination products hide acetaminophen. Total daily acetaminophen must stay within the limit.

HYDROCODONE.clue: Clinical use: opioid usually combined with acetaminophen for short-term pain
HYDROCODONE.rationale: This drug products are controlled. Counsel on constipation, sedation, and the acetaminophen ceiling.

FENTANYL.clue: Clinical use: potent opioid patch that is not for opioid-naive acute pain
FENTANYL.rationale: This drug patches take about a day to reach effect and linger after removal. Heat increases absorption.

METHADONE.clue: Clinical use: long-acting opioid for pain and opioid use disorder that prolongs the QT
METHADONE.rationale: This drug accumulates for days. Dose changes are made slowly, and interacting drugs raise the QT risk.

NALOXONE.clue: Clinical use: opioid antagonist used for overdose, with a shorter duration than many opioids
NALOXONE.rationale: This drug is repeated because respiratory depression can return. It precipitates withdrawal.

NALTREXONE.clue: Clinical use: oral or monthly opioid antagonist for alcohol or opioid use disorder
NALTREXONE.rationale: This drug is not started until opioids have cleared, or it will precipitate withdrawal. It is hepatotoxic at high doses.

TRAMADOL.clue: Clinical use: weak opioid that also raises serotonin and lowers the seizure threshold
TRAMADOL.rationale: This drug plus an SSRI risks serotonin syndrome. Seizure risk rises with high doses and interacting drugs.

MEPERIDINE.clue: Clinical use: opioid avoided chronically because the metabolite normeperidine causes seizures
MEPERIDINE.rationale: This drug with an MAO inhibitor is contraindicated. It is not a preferred pain drug.

CODEINE.clue: Clinical use: prodrug of morphine that is dangerous in ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metabolizers
CODEINE.rationale: This drug is avoided in children after tonsillectomy. Breastfeeding ultra-rapid metabolizers can overdose an infant.

IBUPROFEN.clue: Clinical use: nSAID that can worsen heart failure, kidneys, and ulcers
IBUPROFEN.rationale: This drug blocks COX. It raises blood pressure and blunts the effect of some antihypertensives.

NAPROXEN.clue: Clinical use: longer-acting NSAID with the same renal and gastrointestinal risks
NAPROXEN.rationale: This drug is taken with food. It is avoided in the third trimester because of ductus closure.

KETOROLAC.clue: Clinical use: potent NSAID limited to a few days because of bleeding and kidney injury
KETOROLAC.rationale: This drug is not for chronic pain. The total course, IV plus oral, stays short.

CELECOXIB.clue: Clinical use: cOX-2 inhibitor with less ulcer risk than nonselective NSAIDs but the same heart caution
CELECOXIB.rationale: This drug is a sulfonamide. Cardiovascular risk still applies, and it is not used in significant heart failure.

DICLOFENAC.clue: Clinical use: nSAID available oral and topical, with notable cardiovascular risk
DICLOFENAC.rationale: Topical This drug still has some systemic absorption. Oral This drug is among the higher cardiovascular-risk NSAIDs.

MELOXICAM.clue: Clinical use: once-daily NSAID that is somewhat COX-2 preferring at low doses
MELOXICAM.rationale: This drug is easier to adhere to than ibuprofen. Renal and ulcer warnings remain.

GABAPENTIN.clue: Clinical use: anticonvulsant for neuropathic pain that is renally cleared and sedating
GABAPENTIN.rationale: This drug is titrated. Misuse and respiratory depression with opioids are current warnings.

PREGABALIN.clue: Clinical use: gabapentinoid for neuropathic pain and fibromyalgia that causes edema and dizziness
PREGABALIN.rationale: This drug is a controlled substance. Dose is reduced when creatinine clearance falls.

BACLOFEN.clue: Clinical use: gABA-B agonist for spasticity that can cause seizures if stopped suddenly
BACLOFEN.rationale: Intrathecal This drug withdrawal is an emergency. Oral This drug is tapered.

TIZANIDINE.clue: Clinical use: alpha-2 agonist muscle relaxant that causes hypotension and is affected by CYP1A2 inhibitors
TIZANIDINE.rationale: This drug with ciprofloxacin or fluvoxamine can cause dangerous hypotension. It is hepatotoxic.

SUMATRIPTAN.clue: Clinical use: serotonin agonist for migraine that is contraindicated in coronary disease
SUMATRIPTAN.rationale: This drug is not used within 24 hours of an ergot. Chest pressure can occur even without ischemia.

RIZATRIPTAN.clue: Clinical use: oral triptan whose dose is reduced when propranolol is taken
RIZATRIPTAN.rationale: Propranolol raises This drug levels. The migraine dose is lowered in that combination.

ERGOTAMINE.clue: Clinical use: ergot for migraine that causes severe vasoconstriction with CYP3A4 inhibitors
ERGOTAMINE.rationale: This drug is contraindicated with macrolides and protease inhibitors. It is also contraindicated in pregnancy.

TOPIRAMATE.clue: Clinical use: antiseizure drug used for migraine prevention that causes cognitive slowing and kidney stones
TOPIRAMATE.rationale: This drug is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor. It reduces the effectiveness of estrogen contraceptives at higher doses.

OMEPRAZOLE.clue: Clinical use: proton pump inhibitor taken before breakfast for ulcer and reflux
OMEPRAZOLE.rationale: This drug can lower magnesium and B12 over time and raises C. difficile risk. It inhibits clopidogrel activation.

RABEPRAZOLE.clue: Clinical use: proton pump inhibitor with less CYP2C19 dependence than omeprazole
RABEPRAZOLE.rationale: This drug is an acid-suppression option when a CYP2C19 interaction is a concern.

FAMOTIDINE.clue: Clinical use: h2 blocker adjusted for kidney function
FAMOTIDINE.rationale: This drug does not inhibit CYP enzymes the way cimetidine does. Confusion can occur when the dose is too high for the kidneys.

CIMETIDINE.clue: Clinical use: h2 blocker that inhibits many CYP enzymes and causes antiandrogen effects
CIMETIDINE.rationale: This drug raises levels of warfarin, phenytoin, and other drugs. It is rarely a first H2 blocker now.

SUCRALFATE.clue: Clinical use: ulcer coating agent given on an empty stomach that binds other drugs
SUCRALFATE.rationale: This drug needs acid to work, so it is not paired with continuous acid suppression. Separate interacting drugs.

MISOPROSTOL.clue: Clinical use: prostaglandin that prevents NSAID ulcers and is contraindicated in pregnancy
MISOPROSTOL.rationale: This drug causes uterine contraction. Diarrhea is the limiting side effect.

BISMUTH.clue: Clinical use: agent in some ulcer and diarrhea regimens that blackens the stool and tongue
BISMUTH.rationale: This drug subsalicylate contains salicylate. It is avoided in children with viral illness and in salicylate allergy.

ONDANSETRON.clue: Clinical use: 5-HT3 antiemetic that prolongs the QT interval
ONDANSETRON.rationale: This drug is used for chemotherapy and postoperative nausea. It is not the drug for motion sickness.

GRANISETRON.clue: Clinical use: 5-HT3 antagonist available as a patch for chemotherapy nausea
GRANISETRON.rationale: This drug shares the QT warning of the class. The patch is applied before chemotherapy.

APREPITANT.clue: Clinical use: nK1 antagonist for delayed chemotherapy nausea that interacts with CYP3A4
APREPITANT.rationale: This drug can change the dose needs of dexamethasone and hormonal contraceptives.

DOMPERIDONE.clue: Clinical use: peripheral dopamine antagonist for nausea that prolongs the QT
DOMPERIDONE.rationale: This drug does not cross the blood-brain barrier well, so it causes less central dystonia than metoclopramide.

LOPERAMIDE.clue: Clinical use: opioid antidiarrheal that does not cross the blood-brain barrier at usual doses
LOPERAMIDE.rationale: High-dose This drug abuse causes cardiac arrhythmias. It is not used when fever or bloody stool suggests invasive diarrhea.

DOCUSATE.clue: Clinical use: stool softener that does not stimulate the colon
DOCUSATE.rationale: This drug is for prevention of straining. It will not empty a constipated colon by itself.

SENNA.clue: Clinical use: stimulant laxative used short term or with opioids
SENNA.rationale: This drug causes cramping. Melanosis coli can follow long use and is a marker of chronic stimulant laxatives.

BISACODYL.clue: Clinical use: stimulant laxative tablet that should not be crushed or taken with antacids
BISACODYL.rationale: Enteric This drug dissolves in the colon. Antacids can cause it to release early and irritate the stomach.

LACTULOSE.clue: Clinical use: osmotic laxative that also lowers ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy
LACTULOSE.rationale: This drug is titrated to a few soft stools a day in encephalopathy. Too much causes dehydration.

PSYLLIUM.clue: Clinical use: bulk fiber laxative taken with a full glass of water
PSYLLIUM.rationale: This drug without enough fluid can swell and obstruct. Separate it from other oral drugs.

MESALAMINE.clue: Clinical use: 5-ASA drug for ulcerative colitis, released at different gut sites by formulation
MESALAMINE.rationale: This drug formulations are not interchangeable. Nephrotoxicity is rare but creatinine is checked.

BUDESONIDE.clue: Clinical use: steroid with high first-pass metabolism used for some inflammatory bowel disease
BUDESONIDE.rationale: Oral This drug acts in the gut with less systemic steroid effect than prednisone, but not zero.

INFLIXIMAB.clue: Clinical use: iV TNF inhibitor that can reactivate tuberculosis
