INFLIXIMAB.rationale: This drug requires tuberculosis and hepatitis B screening. Infusion reactions are treated and sometimes premedicated.

ADALIMUMAB.clue: Clinical use: subcutaneous TNF inhibitor with the same infection warnings as infliximab
ADALIMUMAB.rationale: This drug is injected at home. Live vaccines are avoided during therapy.

OCTREOTIDE.clue: Clinical use: somatostatin analog for variceal bleeding and some secretory tumors
OCTREOTIDE.rationale: This drug reduces splanchnic blood flow. It is used with endoscopy, not instead of it, for varices.

URSODIOL.clue: Clinical use: bile acid used to dissolve some gallstones and to treat primary biliary cholangitis
URSODIOL.rationale: This drug is taken with food. It does not dissolve calcified or pigment stones well.

ALBUTEROL.clue: Clinical use: short-acting beta agonist rescue inhaler that causes tremor and tachycardia
ALBUTEROL.rationale: This drug is not a controller. Rising use means the preventive inhaler needs review.

SALMETEROL.clue: Clinical use: long-acting beta agonist that is never used alone in asthma
SALMETEROL.rationale: This drug without an inhaled corticosteroid increases asthma death risk. It is paired with a steroid.

FORMOTEROL.clue: Clinical use: fast-onset long-acting beta agonist used with an inhaled corticosteroid
FORMOTEROL.rationale: This drug can be part of a maintenance-and-reliever regimen. It is not a standalone asthma drug.

TIOTROPIUM.clue: Clinical use: long-acting antimuscarinic inhaler for COPD
TIOTROPIUM.rationale: This drug dries secretions and can cause urinary retention. It is inhaled, not swallowed.

IPRATROPIUM.clue: Clinical use: short-acting antimuscarinic used with albuterol in COPD exacerbations
IPRATROPIUM.rationale: This drug is a reliever. Closed-angle glaucoma can worsen if the mist gets in the eyes.

FLUTICASONE.clue: Clinical use: inhaled corticosteroid that can cause thrush and hoarseness
FLUTICASONE.rationale: Patients rinse and spit after This drug. High doses have some systemic steroid effect.

MOMETASONE.clue: Clinical use: inhaled or nasal corticosteroid for asthma or allergic rhinitis
MOMETASONE.rationale: This drug is a controller or a nasal steroid, not a rescue inhaler.

MONTELUKAST.clue: Clinical use: leukotriene blocker for asthma and allergic rhinitis with a neuropsychiatric warning
MONTELUKAST.rationale: This drug is taken in the evening for asthma. Mood and sleep changes are reported.

ZAFIRLUKAST.clue: Clinical use: leukotriene receptor antagonist taken on an empty stomach
ZAFIRLUKAST.rationale: This drug food reduces absorption. Hepatotoxicity is monitored.

ZILEUTON.clue: Clinical use: 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor for asthma that requires liver monitoring
ZILEUTON.rationale: This drug inhibits theophylline metabolism. ALT is checked.

OMALIZUMAB.clue: Clinical use: anti-IgE injection for allergic asthma given in a setting that can treat anaphylaxis
OMALIZUMAB.rationale: This drug dose depends on weight and IgE level. Patients are observed after injection.

ROFLUMILAST.clue: Clinical use: pDE-4 inhibitor for severe COPD that causes weight loss and psychiatric effects
ROFLUMILAST.rationale: This drug is not a bronchodilator. Diarrhea and weight loss limit its use.

DORNASE.clue: Clinical use: inhaled enzyme that cleaves DNA in cystic fibrosis sputum
DORNASE.rationale: This drug alfa is not mixed with other nebulized drugs in the same cup. It thins infected secretions.

GUAIFENESIN.clue: Clinical use: expectorant taken with water to loosen mucus
GUAIFENESIN.rationale: This drug does not suppress cough. Hydration is part of how it is used.

BENZONATATE.clue: Clinical use: prescription cough capsule that must be swallowed whole
BENZONATATE.rationale: Chewing This drug can numb the mouth and cause choking. It is dangerous in children.

ALLOPURINOL.clue: Clinical use: xanthine oxidase inhibitor for gout prevention, not the treatment of an acute flare alone
ALLOPURINOL.rationale: This drug is titrated to the uric acid goal. A rash can be severe, especially with certain HLA types.

FEBUXOSTAT.clue: Clinical use: xanthine oxidase inhibitor reserved when allopurinol cannot be used
FEBUXOSTAT.rationale: This drug carries a cardiovascular warning. It is still a urate-lowering drug, not an acute-flare drug.

PROBENECID.clue: Clinical use: uricosuric that is avoided in kidney stones and during an acute flare
PROBENECID.rationale: This drug blocks penicillin excretion and raises beta-lactam levels. It needs adequate urine flow.

COLCHICINE.clue: Clinical use: anti-inflammatory for early gout flares that causes diarrhea
COLCHICINE.rationale: This drug dose is reduced with strong CYP3A4 or P-glycoprotein inhibitors and in kidney disease.

PEGLICASE.clue: Clinical use: iV uricase for refractory gout that can cause infusion reactions
PEGLICASE.rationale: Pegloticase is stopped if uric acid rises, because that signals antibody formation and a higher reaction risk.

LEFLUNOMIDE.clue: Clinical use: dMARD with a very long half-life that is teratogenic
LEFLUNOMIDE.rationale: This drug is washed out with cholestyramine when pregnancy is planned. Liver enzymes are monitored.

TACROLIMUS.clue: Clinical use: calcineurin inhibitor with a narrow index, nephrotoxicity, and CYP3A4 interactions
TACROLIMUS.rationale: This drug levels are troughs. Grapefruit and many antifungals raise the level.

SIROLIMUS.clue: Clinical use: mTOR inhibitor that impairs wound healing and raises lipids
SIROLIMUS.rationale: This drug is not started immediately around major surgery if healing is the priority. Mouth ulcers are common.

FILGRASTIM.clue: Clinical use: g-CSF that raises neutrophils and causes bone pain
FILGRASTIM.rationale: This drug is timed after chemotherapy so it does not stimulate cells still being killed. It is not a chemotherapy drug.

MESNA.clue: Clinical use: uroprotectant given with ifosfamide or high-dose cyclophosphamide
MESNA.rationale: This drug binds acrolein in the bladder. Hemorrhagic cystitis is the toxicity it prevents.

LEUCOVORIN.clue: Clinical use: reduced folate that rescues normal cells after methotrexate
LEUCOVORIN.rationale: This drug timing matters. It is also given to boost fluorouracil in some colorectal regimens.

RASBURICASE.clue: Clinical use: uricase for tumor lysis that is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency
RASBURICASE.rationale: This drug makes uric acid samples fall in the tube. The lab must handle the specimen on ice.

DEXRAZOXANE.clue: Clinical use: chelator that reduces anthracycline heart injury and is also an extravasation antidote
DEXRAZOXANE.rationale: This drug is not routine for every doxorubicin patient. It is used when the cumulative dose is high or for extravasation.

TAMOXIFEN.clue: Clinical use: sERM for estrogen-receptor breast cancer that raises clot and endometrial risk
TAMOXIFEN.rationale: This drug is a prodrug via CYP2D6. Strong CYP2D6 inhibitors such as paroxetine can reduce its activation.

ANASTROZOLE.clue: Clinical use: aromatase inhibitor for postmenopausal hormone-receptor breast cancer
ANASTROZOLE.rationale: This drug causes joint pain and bone loss. It is not the adjuvant endocrine drug for a premenopausal woman alone.

LETROZOLE.clue: Clinical use: aromatase inhibitor used in postmenopausal breast cancer and some fertility protocols
LETROZOLE.rationale: This drug lowers estrogen. Bone density and cholesterol are followed in long adjuvant use.

IMATINIB.clue: Clinical use: bCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor taken with food and a large glass of water
IMATINIB.rationale: This drug causes edema and muscle cramps. CYP3A4 inducers lower its level.

ERLOTINIB.clue: Clinical use: eGFR inhibitor taken on an empty stomach that causes an acneiform rash
ERLOTINIB.rationale: This drug rash is a class effect. Proton pump inhibitors markedly reduce its absorption.

HYDROXYUREA.clue: Clinical use: ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor for sickle cell disease and some myeloproliferative disease
HYDROXYUREA.rationale: This drug raises fetal hemoglobin in sickle cell disease. Blood counts are followed because it is myelosuppressive.

GRAPEFRUIT.clue: Clinical use: fruit that inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 and raises levels of many drugs
GRAPEFRUIT.rationale: This drug juice is a one-way interaction: it inhibits, it does not induce. The effect can last more than a day.

TYRAMINE.clue: Clinical use: dietary amine that causes hypertensive crisis with MAO inhibitors
TYRAMINE.rationale: Aged cheese, cured meats, and tap beer are high in This drug. Patients on phenelzine need this list.

ALCOHOL.clue: Clinical use: cNS depressant that causes a disulfiram reaction with metronidazole and tinidazole
ALCOHOL.rationale: This drug adds sedation to opioids and benzodiazepines and liver risk to acetaminophen in heavy use.

CHARCOAL.clue: Clinical use: adsorbent used for some recent overdoses that binds other oral drugs
CHARCOAL.rationale: Activated This drug does not bind iron, lithium, or alcohols well. The airway must be protected.

ANTACID.clue: Clinical use: magnesium, aluminum, or calcium product that chelates quinolones and tetracyclines
ANTACID.rationale: Separate antacids from levothyroxine, quinolones, and tetracyclines by several hours.

CHELATION.clue: Clinical use: binding of a drug by calcium, iron, or magnesium that blocks absorption
CHELATION.rationale: This drug is why ciprofloxacin and doxycycline are separated from dairy and supplements.

PRODRUG.clue: Clinical use: inactive compound that must be converted to the active drug
PRODRUG.rationale: Clopidogrel and codeine are prodrugs. Poor metabolizers may get little effect.

FIRSTPASS.clue: Clinical use: liver metabolism of an oral drug before it reaches the circulation
FIRSTPASS.rationale: High first-pass extraction is why some drugs are given IV or as patches. Inhibitors of that path raise levels.

HALFLIFE.clue: Clinical use: time for the plasma concentration to fall by half, used to estimate steady state
HALFLIFE.rationale: About four to five half-lives are needed to reach steady state. A long half-life means a long washout.

CLEARANCE.clue: Clinical use: volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time
CLEARANCE.rationale: This drug falls in the organ that eliminates the drug. Dose rate is This drug times target concentration.

TROUGH.clue: Clinical use: concentration drawn just before the next dose
TROUGH.rationale: Aminoglycoside and vancomycin troughs, or AUC, are used to limit toxicity.

PEAK.clue: Clinical use: concentration drawn after distribution, reflecting the highest level
PEAK.rationale: Peaks are timed after the infusion ends, not during it. They are used for some aminoglycoside regimens.

BIOEQUIV.clue: Clinical use: standard showing a generic delivers the same exposure as the reference product
BIOEQUIV.rationale: Bioequivalence uses AUC and peak concentration limits. Narrow-therapeutic-index drugs are sometimes debated.

SUBLINGUAL.clue: Clinical use: route that bypasses the gut and first-pass liver metabolism
SUBLINGUAL.rationale: Nitroglycerin tablets are not swallowed. The patient sits, because the blood pressure will fall.

TRANSDERMAL.clue: Clinical use: patch route that gives steady absorption and lingers after removal
TRANSDERMAL.rationale: Fentanyl and clonidine patches are folded and discarded safely. Heat increases absorption.

ENTERIC.clue: Clinical use: coating that keeps a tablet from dissolving in the stomach
ENTERIC.rationale: This drug tablets are not crushed. Bisacodyl and some aspirin products depend on the coating.

INDUCER.clue: Clinical use: drug that increases enzyme activity and lowers substrate levels
INDUCER.rationale: Rifampin, carbamazepine, and phenytoin are classic inducers. The effect takes days to appear and to wear off.

INHIBITOR.clue: Clinical use: drug that blocks an enzyme and raises substrate levels
INHIBITOR.rationale: Azoles, macrolides, and ritonavir inhibit CYP3A4. The interaction can appear with the first doses.

SUBSTRATE.clue: Clinical use: drug that is metabolized by a given enzyme
SUBSTRATE.rationale: A This drug's level rises with an inhibitor and falls with an inducer of its enzyme.

PHENYTOIN.clue: Clinical use: antiseizure drug with nonlinear kinetics and a high protein binding
PHENYTOIN.rationale: This drug small dose changes cause large level changes near the therapeutic range. Low albumin raises the free fraction.

DISULFIRAM.clue: Clinical use: alcohol-deterrent drug that causes flushing and vomiting if ethanol is consumed
DISULFIRAM.rationale: This drug blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase. Hidden alcohol in mouthwash and sauces can trigger the reaction.

NALMEFENE.clue: Clinical use: opioid antagonist related to naloxone with a longer duration in some formulations
NALMEFENE.rationale: Opioid antagonists reverse respiratory depression and can precipitate acute withdrawal.

FOMEPIZOLE.clue: Clinical use: alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor for methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning
FOMEPIZOLE.rationale: This drug blocks formation of toxic metabolites. It is preferred over ethanol when available.

GLUCAGON.clue: Clinical use: hormone used for beta-blocker overdose and for severe hypoglycemia when the patient cannot swallow
GLUCAGON.rationale: This drug raises glucose from liver stores. It will not work well if glycogen is depleted.

SUCCIMER.clue: Clinical use: oral chelator for lead poisoning
SUCCIMER.rationale: This drug is used when the lead level and the clinical picture meet treatment thresholds. It chelates other metals too.

PRALIDOXIME.clue: Clinical use: cholinesterase reactivator given with atropine for organophosphate poisoning
PRALIDOXIME.rationale: This drug works best before the enzyme ages. Atropine treats the muscarinic symptoms.

DIGIFAB.clue: Clinical use: antibody fragments that bind digoxin for life-threatening toxicity
DIGIFAB.rationale: Digoxin immune fab is dosed by the amount ingested or the level. The level after treatment is not interpretable.

SUGAMMADEX.clue: Clinical use: reversal agent that encapsulates rocuronium and vecuronium
SUGAMMADEX.rationale: This drug can bind hormonal contraceptives for a week. It is not a reversal for succinylcholine.

VITAMINK.clue: Clinical use: fat-soluble vitamin that reverses warfarin and must be consistent in the diet
VITAMINK.rationale: Patients do not avoid greens; they keep the intake steady. Pharmaceutical vitamin K is phytonadione.

ORANGEBOOK.clue: Clinical use: fDA reference that rates therapeutic equivalence of generic products
ORANGEBOOK.rationale: An AB rating means the generic is therapeutically equivalent to the reference. Other codes flag unresolved issues.

AUXLABEL.clue: Clinical use: extra sticker that carries a critical counseling point the vial label may not emphasize
AUXLABEL.rationale: Auxiliary labels cover shake well, take with food, and do not crush. They do not replace spoken counseling.

NDCNUMBER.clue: Clinical use: identifier on the package used to pick the correct product at the shelf
NDCNUMBER.rationale: The NDC is not a substitute for reading the drug name and strength. Look-alike packages are a known error source.

TALLMAN.clue: Clinical use: mixed-case lettering that separates look-alike drug names
TALLMAN.rationale: Tall-man letters highlight the dissimilar part of names such as hydrOXYzine and hydrALAZINE.

HIGHALERT.clue: Clinical use: category that includes insulin, opioids, anticoagulants, and concentrated electrolytes
HIGHALERT.rationale: High-alert drugs need independent checks. A tenfold insulin or heparin error is a classic harm.

ISMP.clue: Clinical use: organization that publishes high-alert lists and error-prevention standards
ISMP.rationale: This drug recommendations drive tall-man letters, do-not-crush lists, and standard concentrations.

BEERS.clue: Clinical use: criteria that list drugs to avoid or dose-reduce in older adults
BEERS.rationale: The This drug list flags glyburide, many anticholinergics, and sliding-scale insulin as higher risk in older adults.

ANTICHOLIN.clue: Clinical use: effect that causes dry mouth, constipation, retention, and confusion
ANTICHOLIN.rationale: Anticholinergic burden adds up across drugs. Older adults are especially vulnerable to delirium.

QTPROLONG.clue: Clinical use: effect that raises torsades risk, worsened by low potassium or magnesium
QTPROLONG.rationale: Ondansetron, citalopram, and many antipsychotics prolong the QT. Correct electrolytes and avoid stacking them.

SEROTONIN.clue: Clinical use: syndrome of clonus, hyperreflexia, and agitation from stacked serotonergic drugs
SEROTONIN.rationale: This drug syndrome is neuromuscular hyperactivity. It is not the same as neuroleptic malignant syndrome rigidity.

NARROWTI.clue: Clinical use: therapeutic index small enough that levels or close monitoring are required
NARROWTI.rationale: Narrow therapeutic index drugs include warfarin, lithium, phenytoin, and digoxin.

CREATININE.clue: Clinical use: lab used to estimate kidney function for renal dosing
CREATININE.rationale: This drug clearance equations need a stable This drug, age, weight, and sex. They overestimate function in frail patients.

COCKCROFT.clue: Clinical use: equation that estimates creatinine clearance from age, weight, sex, and creatinine
COCKCROFT.rationale: The This drug-Gault equation is still used in many drug labels. Use actual, ideal, or adjusted weight as the label directs.

IDEALWT.clue: Clinical use: weight based on height and sex, used in some clearance and dose calculations
IDEALWT.rationale: Ideal body weight avoids overdosing renally cleared drugs in patients with obesity when the label says to use it.

BSA.clue: Clinical use: body surface area used to dose many chemotherapy drugs
BSA.rationale: This drug dosing uses height and weight. Recalculate it; do not copy an old value after a large weight change.

MILLIMOLE.clue: Clinical use: unit of amount used for electrolytes such as phosphate and some potassium orders
MILLIMOLE.rationale: Millimoles and milliequivalents are not identical for divalent ions. Read the phosphate order units carefully.

OSMOLARITY.clue: Clinical use: concentration term used to judge whether an IV fluid is isotonic
OSMOLARITY.rationale: Hyperosmolar infusions through a small vein cause phlebitis. Parenteral nutrition This drug limits peripheral use.

ALLIGATION.clue: Clinical use: method for mixing two concentrations to reach a desired strength
ALLIGATION.rationale: This drug solves how many parts of each strength to combine. It does not replace checking the final volume.

DROPS.clue: Clinical use: volume unit for ophthalmic and some oral liquids, which is not exactly a milliliter
DROPS.rationale: A dropper is calibrated to its bottle. Do not substitute a household teaspoon for a measured oral syringe.

INFUSION.clue: Clinical use: intravenous delivery calculated from concentration, rate, and time
INFUSION.rationale: This drug rate errors are prevented by standard concentrations and an independent check of the pump.

CRUSH.clue: Clinical use: instruction that is unsafe for extended-release, enteric, and hazardous tablets
CRUSH.rationale: Do-not-This drug lists include bupropion XL, bisacodyl, and many oncology drugs. Open a capsule only if the label allows it.

HAZARDOUS.clue: Clinical use: drug category that includes chemotherapy and requires special handling
HAZARDOUS.rationale: This drug drugs are not crushed on an open counter. Pregnant staff follow the facility handling policy.

REMS.clue: Clinical use: fDA program that restricts distribution of drugs with serious risks
REMS.rationale: Isotretinoin and clozapine are examples of drugs with required monitoring programs. A prescription alone may not be enough to dispense.

TRETINOIN.clue: Clinical use: topical retinoid for acne that is photosensitizing and not the oral teratogen
TRETINOIN.rationale: Topical This drug is not isotretinoin. It still irritates skin and is avoided in pregnancy by many clinicians.

BENZOYL.clue: Clinical use: topical antibacterial for acne that bleaches fabric
BENZOYL.rationale: This drug peroxide can inactivate tretinoin if they are applied at the same moment. Many regimens separate them.

ADAPALENE.clue: Clinical use: topical retinoid available over the counter for acne
ADAPALENE.rationale: This drug causes dryness and sun sensitivity. Benefit takes weeks.

HYDROCORT.clue: Clinical use: low-potency topical steroid safe enough for limited face and fold use
HYDROCORT.rationale: Hydrocortisone is the mild end of the topical steroid ladder. Potent steroids are not used on the face chronically.

CLOBETASOL.clue: Clinical use: super-potent topical steroid limited to short courses
CLOBETASOL.rationale: This drug can thin skin and suppress the adrenal axis if it is used on large areas for long periods.

MUPIROCIN.clue: Clinical use: topical antibiotic for impetigo and nasal decolonization
MUPIROCIN.rationale: This drug ointment is applied to lesions. The nasal form is for staph carriage protocols, not routine cuts.

LIDOCAINE.clue: Clinical use: local anesthetic patch or gel with a maximum daily dose because of seizures and arrhythmias
LIDOCAINE.rationale: This drug patches are worn for 12 hours and off for 12. Do not cover them with heat.

CAPSAICIN.clue: Clinical use: topical chili derivative for neuropathic pain that burns at first
CAPSAICIN.rationale: This drug is applied with gloves. Hands are washed so the drug is not transferred to the eyes.

MENTHOL.clue: Clinical use: counterirritant in many topical pain products
MENTHOL.rationale: This drug feels cool. Combination patches still count toward the lidocaine or salicylate dose if those are included.

VARENICLINE.clue: Clinical use: partial nicotine agonist for smoking cessation that can change mood
VARENICLINE.rationale: This drug is titrated to reduce nausea. Psychiatric history is discussed, and vivid dreams are common.

NICOTINE.clue: Clinical use: replacement therapy that is not smoked and is dosed to withdrawal symptoms
NICOTINE.rationale: This drug gum is chewed and parked. The patch is removed at night if insomnia or vivid dreams occur.
